title: A Modest Proposal
input:
To prevent the children of impoverished families in Ireland from becoming a burden on their parents or society, and to ensure they contribute positively to the public good, attention must be directed toward their situation. 

It is a sorrowful sight for those who walk through the city or travel in the countryside. They observe the streets, roads, and doorways crowded with female beggars accompanied by three, four, or even six ragged children. These mothers are unable to earn a legitimate income and must dedicate all their time to begging for food to support their vulnerable infants. As these children grow, they often resort to theft due to a lack of employment opportunities, leave their homeland to fight for the Pretender in Spain, or sell themselves into servitude in the Caribbean.
human:
For preventing the children of poor people in Ireland, from being a burden on their parents or country, and for making them beneficial to the publick.

It is a melancholy object to those, who walk through this great town, or travel in the country, when they see the streets, the roads, and cabbin-doors crowded with beggars of the female sex, followed by three, four, or six children, all in rags, and importuning every passenger for an alms. These mothers, instead of being able to work for their honest livelihood, are forced to employ all their time in stroling to beg sustenance for their helpless infants who, as they grow up, either turn thieves for want of work, or leave their dear native country, to fight for the Pretender in Spain, or sell themselves to the Barbadoes.
base:
To prevent the children of poor families in Ireland from becoming a burden on their parents or society, and to make sure they help the community, people need to focus on their situation.  

It’s a sad thing to see when you walk through the city or travel in the countryside. You see the streets, the roads, the doorways filled with women begging with three, four, or even six thin children. These mothers can’t earn money the right way and have to spend all their time asking for food to feed their weak babies. As the kids get older, they often steal because there’s no work, or they leave home to fight for the Pretender in Spain, or they sell themselves in the Caribbean.
finetuned:
“The poor children of the beggarly poor in Ireland, to make them not a charge on their parents or on the society, and to make them a benefit to the public good, we must look to their case.

It is a melancholy sight to see a man walk in the city, or travel through the country, to see the streets and roads and doorways full of female beggars with three, four, or six ragged children. These poor mothers cannot get a lawful livelihood, and must spend all their time in begging for food for their helpless infants. When they grow they steal, or leave their country to fight for the Pretender in Spain, or sell themselves into slavery in the West Indies.”

title: A Modest Proposal
input:
Individuals who are more frugal, which the current times necessitate, may utilize the carcass in its entirety. The skin, when properly treated, can be transformed into excellent gloves for women and summer boots for men. 

Regarding the City of Dublin, suitable locations can be designated for this purpose in the most accessible areas. There will certainly be no shortage of butchers available. However, I suggest purchasing the children while they are still alive and preparing them immediately after slaughter, similar to the way we prepare roasted pigs.
human:
Those who are more thrifty (as I must confess the times require) may flay the carcass; the skin of which, artificially dressed, will make admirable gloves for ladies, and summer boots for fine gentlemen.

As to our City of Dublin, shambles may be appointed for this purpose, in the most convenient parts of it, and butchers we may be assured will not be wanting; although I rather recommend buying the children alive, and dressing them hot from the knife, as we do roasting pigs.

title: A Modest Proposal
input:
I am assured by our merchants that a child, whether male or female, under the age of twelve years is not a marketable commodity. Furthermore, even upon reaching this age, such individuals will not fetch more than three pounds, or at most three pounds and half a crown in the marketplace. This situation proves disadvantageous for both the parents and the kingdom, as the expenses of sustenance and clothing have amounted to at least four times that value. 

In essence, I shall now humbly present my own thoughts on the matter, which I trust will not encounter any objections.
human:

I shall now therefore humbly propose my own thoughts, which I hope will not be liable to the least objection.

title: A Modest Proposal
input: It is widely acknowledged by all involved that the considerable number of children being carried in the arms, on the backs, or trailing behind their mothers, and often their fathers, represents a significant additional grievance within the current lamentable state of the kingdom. Furthermore, anyone who could devise a just, economical, and straightforward approach to transforming these children into healthy and valuable members of the commonwealth would merit exceptional recognition from the public, potentially warranting the erection of a statue in their honor as a preserver of the nation.

Anyone who can find a fair, cost-effective, and simple way to turn these children into healthy, useful members of society would be highly praised by the people. Such a person might even be honored with a statue as a protector of the nation.

title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
input:
They approached the Mock Turtle, who regarded them with tearful eyes but remained silent. 

They took a seat, and for several moments, no one spoke. Alice contemplated the situation, thinking it unlikely for him to conclude without starting. Nevertheless, she chose to remain patient.

This led to a prolonged silence, interrupted occasionally by the Gryphon's outbursts of "Hjckrrh!" and the Mock Turtle's continuous weeping. Alice almost stood up to express her gratitude for what she perceived as an interesting story, yet she held back, sensing that there might be more to hear, so she remained quiet.
human:
So they went up to the Mock Turtle, who looked at them with large eyes full of tears, but said nothing.

So they sat down, and nobody spoke for some minutes. Alice thought to herself, “I don’t see how he can ever finish, if he doesn’t begin.” But she waited patiently.

These words were followed by a very long silence, broken only by an occasional exclamation of “Hjckrrh!” from the Gryphon, and the constant heavy sobbing of the Mock Turtle. Alice was very nearly getting up and saying, “Thank you, sir, for your interesting story,” but she could not help thinking there must be more to come, so she sat still and said nothing.
base:
They approached the Mock Turtle, who looked at them with tearful eyes but said nothing.  

They sat down, and for a while, no one spoke. Alice thought about the situation, wondering if he would finish without beginning. But she stayed patient anyway.  

The silence stretched on, broken now and then by the Gryphon's "Hjckrrh!" and the Mock Turtle's constant crying. Alice almost stood up to thank him for the story she thought was interesting, but she stayed seated, feeling there was more to come.
finetuned:
They went up to the Mock Turtle, who looked at them with tearful eyes, but made no reply.

They sat down, and for some minutes nobody spoke. Alice was thinking, “It’s quite certain he’ll not end without beginning;” but she was too good-natured to be impatient.

So there was a long silence, which was occasionally broken by the Gryphon’s “Hjckrrh!” and the Mock Turtle’s continual weeping. Alice quite wished to get up and thank him for the very nice story he was telling, but she restrained herself, for she thought there might be something more to come, so she said nothing.

title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
input:
An enormous puppy gazed down at her with large, round eyes, and feebly extended one paw, attempting to make contact with her. "Poor little creature!" remarked Alice in a coaxing tone, as she earnestly attempted to whistle to it; however, she was persistently terrified at the thought that it might be hungry, which could result in its consuming her despite her efforts at coaxing.

Barely aware of her actions, she picked up a small stick and offered it to the puppy. Consequently, the puppy leaped into the air, propelling itself off all four feet simultaneously with a delighted yelp, and rushed towards the stick, feigning an intent to worry it. In response, Alice sought refuge behind a large thistle to avoid being overwhelmed. The moment she reappeared on the opposite side, the puppy made another dash for the stick, tumbling head over heels in its eagerness to seize it. Alice, perceiving the situation as reminiscent of engaging in play with a cart-horse and anticipating the imminent possibility of being trampled, circled back around the thistle. Subsequently, the puppy initiated a series of brief charges toward the stick, moving only a short distance forward each time while retreating a considerable distance back, all the while barking hoarsely. Eventually, it settled down at a distance, panting, with its tongue lolling out of its mouth and its large eyes partially closed.

Hardly knowing what she did, she picked up a little bit of stick, and held it out to the puppy; whereupon the puppy jumped into the air off all its feet at once, with a yelp of delight, and rushed at the stick, and made believe to worry it; then Alice dodged behind a great thistle, to keep herself from being run over; and the moment she appeared on the other side, the puppy made another rush at the stick, and tumbled head over heels in its hurry to get hold of it; then Alice, thinking it was very like having a game of play with a cart-horse, and expecting every moment to be trampled under its feet, ran round the thistle again; then the puppy began a series of short charges at the stick, running a very little way forwards each time and a long way back, and barking hoarsely all the while, till at last it sat down a good way off, panting, with its tongue hanging out of its mouth, and its great eyes half shut.

She went around the thistle again. The puppy then ran short bursts toward the stick, moving forward a little and back a lot, barking loudly. Finally, it stopped a ways away, breathing hard, tongue hanging out, and eyes half-closed.

title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
input: Alice encountered some challenges at the beginning, particularly with her flamingo. She managed to secure its body comfortably under her arm, allowing its legs to dangle down, but typically, just as she had the neck positioned straight, and was ready to strike the hedgehog, the flamingo would twist around to gaze up at her with a confused expression. This often made her laugh. When she finally got its head back down and prepared to try again, it could be quite frustrating to find that the hedgehog had rolled itself up and was attempting to crawl away. Additionally, there were often obstacles in the form of ridges or furrows that got in the way of where she wanted to direct the hedgehog. Given that the soldiers nearby were frequently standing up and moving to different spots, Alice soon realized that this game was quite challenging. Overall, her experience illustrated how complicated the situation could be.

title: The Secret Garden
input:
Mr. Craven may have managed to extend his arms just in time to prevent a fall during an unexpected encounter, and as he held the boy away to look at him in surprise at his presence, he found himself slightly breathless. 

The boy was tall and quite attractive, radiating vitality, and his energetic run had brought a vibrant flush to his cheeks. He pushed his thick hair back from his forehead and raised a pair of unusual gray eyes—eyes that seemed to sparkle with youthful joy and were framed by dark lashes. It was likely those eyes that left Mr. Craven momentarily astonished. In summary, the boy’s lively appearance and striking gaze created a memorable impression on Mr. Craven.

title: The Secret Garden
input: Mary received her meals consistently, with Martha serving her, but there was a noticeable lack of concern for her well-being. Mrs. Medlock visited every few days to check on her, yet no one engaged with her about her activities or provided guidance on what she should do. This situation led Mary to believe that it might be typical in England to treat children this way. In India, she had always been attended to by her Ayah, who was constantly by her side and catered to her needs. While she sometimes found her presence tiresome, the contrast to her current situation was stark. Now, she was alone and beginning to learn how to dress herself, as Martha often looked at her with a sense of disapproval when she requested assistance.
human: Mary’s meals were served regularly, and Martha waited on her, but no one troubled themselves about her in the least. Mrs. Medlock came and looked at her every day or two, but no one inquired what she did or told her what to do. She supposed that perhaps this was the English way of treating children. In India she had always been attended by her Ayah, who had followed her about and waited on her, hand and foot. She had often been tired of her company. Now she was followed by nobody and was learning to dress herself because Martha looked as though she thought she was silly and stupid when she wanted to have things handed to her and put on.

title: The Secret Garden
input:
He very seldom engaged in conversation and at times did not even respond to Mary’s inquiries, except with a grunt; however, this morning he spoke more than usual. He stood up and placed one hobnailed boot upon the top of his spade while he scanned her appearance.

Moreover, it is worth noting that Mary was not vain, and since she had never given much consideration to her looks, she was not significantly disturbed by the observation.

“I am aware that I have gained weight,” she remarked. “My stockings are becoming tighter. They used to create wrinkles. There is the robin, Ben Weatherstaff.”

title: Treasure Island
input: I opened my eyes immediately. All around me were small ripples, moving over with a sharp, bristling sound and a slight phosphorescence. The HISPANIOLA herself, a few yards in whose wake I was still being carried along, appeared to stagger in her course, and I observed her spars toss a little against the darkness of the night; indeed, as I looked longer, I became certain that she was also turning toward the south. I glanced over my shoulder, and my heart leaped against my ribs. There, directly behind me, was the glow of the camp-fire. The current had turned at right angles, sweeping along with it the tall schooner and the small dancing coracle; ever accelerating, ever rising higher, ever murmuring more loudly, it went spinning through the narrows toward the open sea.

In the meantime, there was no doubt regarding one particular matter; they maintained an exceedingly poor watch. If it had been Silver and his crew who were now approaching them, not a single individual would have witnessed the dawn. That was the unfortunate consequence of having the captain injured, and once again, I chastised myself for leaving them in such peril with so few individuals on guard.

By this point, I had arrived at the door and stood up. The interior was completely dark, preventing me from perceiving anything with my eyes. In terms of auditory perceptions, there was the continuous drone of individuals snoring, accompanied by a small, intermittent sound, a flickering or pecking noise that I could not explain in any manner.

title: Treasure Island
input: Of the eight men who had fallen during the battle, only three remained alive: one pirate who had been shot at the loophole, Hunter, and Captain Smollett. However, the first two were effectively beyond saving. The mutineer succumbed to his injuries under the doctor's care, while Hunter, despite our best efforts, never regained consciousness. He struggled throughout the day, breathing heavily like an old buccaneer suffering from an apoplectic fit. Unfortunately, his chest had been crushed by the impact, and his skull was fractured from the fall. Sometime during the following night, without any sign or sound, he passed away.

He lingered all day, breathing loudly like the old buccaneer at home in his apoplectic fit, but the bones of his chest had been crushed by the blow and his skull fractured in falling, and some time in the following night, without sign or sound, he went to his Maker.

Later that night, without a sound, he died.

title: Treasure Island
input: It is worth noting that the island's appearance may have contributed to my feelings; its somber, grey woods and rugged stone spires, coupled with the sound of the surf crashing and foaming on the steep beach, created an overwhelmingly melancholic atmosphere. Furthermore, despite the bright and scorching sun and the shore birds fishing and calling around us, one might have assumed that anyone would be pleased to reach land after an extended period at sea. However, my heart sank considerably, as the expression goes, and from that initial glance onward, I developed a profound dislike for the mere thought of Treasure Island.
human: Perhaps it was this - perhaps it was the look of the island, with its grey, melancholy woods, and wild stone spires, and the surf that we could both see and hear foaming and thundering on the steep beach - at least, although the sun shone bright and hot, and the shore birds were fishing and crying all around us, and you would have thought anyone would have been glad to get to land after being so long at sea, my heart sank, as the saying is, into my boots; and from the first look onward, I hated the very thought of Treasure Island.

title: On the Origin of Species
input: The eyes of moles and certain burrowing rodents are rudimentary in size, and in some cases they are entirely covered by skin and fur. This condition of the eyes is probably the result of gradual reduction through disuse, although it may also have been aided by natural selection. In South America, a burrowing rodent known as the tuco-tuco, or Ctenomys, is even more subterranean in its habits than the mole. A Spaniard who had often caught these animals assured me that they were frequently blind. One that I kept alive was certainly in this condition, and dissection showed that the cause was inflammation of the nictitating membrane. Since frequent inflammation of the eyes must be harmful to any animal, and since eyes are certainly not indispensable to animals with subterranean habits, a reduction in their size, together with the adhesion of the eyelids and the growth of fur over them, might in such a case be an advantage. If this were so, natural selection would constantly aid the effects of disuse.

title: On the Origin of Species
input: In the case of animals with separate sexes, the capacity to prevent crosses constitutes an important element of success in the formation of new races, at least in a country that is already stocked with other races. Additionally, in this respect the enclosure of the land plays a part. Moreover, wandering savages or the inhabitants of open plains rarely possess more than one breed of the same species. Furthermore, pigeons can be mated for life, and this is a great convenience to the fancier, for in this manner many races may be kept true, though mingled in the same aviary, and this circumstance must have largely favoured the improvement and formation of new breeds. It is worth noting that pigeons, I may add, can be propagated in great numbers and at a very quick rate, and inferior birds may be freely rejected, since when killed they serve for food. In essence, on the other hand, cats, from their nocturnal rambling habits, cannot be matched, and, although so much valued by women and children, we hardly ever see a distinct breed kept up; such breeds as we do sometimes see are almost always imported from some other country, often from islands. Additionally, although I do not doubt that some domestic animals vary less than others, yet the rarity or absence of distinct breeds of the cat, the donkey, peacock, goose, and so forth, may be attributed in main part to selection not having been brought into play: in cats, from the difficulty in pairing them; in donkeys, from only a few being kept by poor people, and little attention paid to their breeding; in peacocks, from not being very easily reared and a large stock not kept; in geese, from being valuable only for two purposes, food and feathers, and more especially from no pleasure having been felt in the display of distinct breeds.

title: On the Origin of Species
input: This highlights the observation that we know nothing about the origin or history of any of our domestic breeds. In reality, a breed, much like a dialect of a language, can hardly be said to have had a definite origin. A man preserves and breeds from an individual with some slight deviation of structure, or takes more care than usual in matching his best animals, thereby improving them, and the improved individuals slowly spread in the immediate neighbourhood. At this stage, however, they will hardly have a distinct name, and since they are only slightly valued, their history will be disregarded. When further improved through the same slow and gradual process, they will spread more widely and come to be recognised as something distinct and valuable, and will then probably first receive a provincial name. In semi-civilised countries with little free communication, the spreading and knowledge of any new sub-breed will be a slow process. Once the points of value of the new sub-breed are fully acknowledged, the principle of unconscious selection will always tend to slowly add to the characteristic features of the breed, whatever they may be, perhaps more at one period than another as the breed rises or falls in fashion, and perhaps more in one district than another according to the state of civilisation of the inhabitants. Ultimately, the chance of any record having been preserved of such slow, varying, and insensible changes will be infinitely small.
human: I think these views further explain what has sometimes been noticed - namely that we know nothing about the origin or history of any of our domestic breeds. But, in fact, a breed, like a dialect of a language, can hardly be said to have had a definite origin. When further improved by the same slow and gradual process, they will spread more widely, and will get recognised as something distinct and valuable, and will then probably first receive a provincial name. In semi-civilised countries, with little free communication, the spreading and knowledge of any new sub-breed will be a slow process. As soon as the points of value of the new sub-breed are once fully acknowledged, the principle, as I have called it, of unconscious selection will always tend, - perhaps more at one period than at another, as the breed rises or falls in fashion, - perhaps more in one district than in another, according to the state of civilisation of the inhabitants - slowly to add to the characteristic features of the breed, whatever they may be. But the chance will be infinitely small of any record having been preserved of such slow, varying, and insensible changes.

title: On the Origin of Species
input: It is important to note that the process may not occur as consistently as illustrated in the diagram, even if it is somewhat irregular. It is not necessarily the case that the most distinct varieties will always dominate and reproduce; a more moderate form may often persist for extended periods and might or might not lead to more than one altered descendant. Natural selection typically operates based on the specific characteristics of environments that are either unoccupied or not fully occupied by other organisms, which can be influenced by a multitude of complex interactions. Generally speaking, the more varied in structure the descendants from a single species can become, the better their chances of exploiting different niches, which may lead to an increase in their modified offspring. In the diagram, the line of succession appears to be interrupted at regular intervals, indicated by small numbered letters that represent the distinct forms recognized as varieties. However, these interruptions are theoretical and could have been placed at various points, assuming sufficient time for significant divergent variation to accumulate. Overall, the complexity of these processes highlights the nuanced nature of evolutionary change.
human: But I must here remark that I do not suppose that the process ever goes on so regularly as is represented in the diagram, though in itself made somewhat irregular. I am far from thinking that the most divergent varieties will invariably prevail and multiply: a medium form may often long endure, and may or may not produce more than one modified descendant; for natural selection will always act according to the nature of the places which are either unoccupied or not perfectly occupied by other beings; and this will depend on infinitely complex relations. But as a general rule, the more diversified in structure the descendants from any one species can be rendered, the more places they will be enabled to seize on, and the more their modified progeny will be increased. In our diagram the line of succession is broken at regular intervals by small numbered letters marking the successive forms which have become sufficiently distinct to be recorded as varieties. But these breaks are imaginary, and might have been inserted anywhere, after intervals long enough to have allowed the accumulation of a considerable amount of divergent variation.
base: The diagram shows a process that may not happen as regularly as it appears. Some forms might not always be the most distinct; a less extreme one could stay around for a long time and maybe produce several different versions. Natural selection depends on the specific traits of places that aren’t fully filled by other life, and that’s shaped by many different factors. The more different a group of creatures can become, the better they can fit into different roles, which might make their changes more likely. In the diagram, the line of change stops at regular spots, marked by small letters showing the different forms called varieties. But these breaks are just ideas—they could have happened anywhere if there was enough time for big changes to happen. All together, these things show how complex and subtle evolution really is.
finetuned: But, as I have already remarked, the diagram is not to be taken as representing the exact or even as approximately representing the true mode of succession. For it is not necessarily the case that the most distinct varieties will always reign and multiply; but a more moderate form will often endure for ages, and may or may not give rise to more than one modified descendant. Natural selection acts, as we may say, on the actual structure of the environment, whether unoccupied or only partially occupied by other organisms; and the structure of the environment is determined by an infinite number of complex relations. The more structurally varied the descendants from a single species become, the more chance they have of exploiting new niches, and hence the more likely they are to give rise to modified descendants. In the diagram the line of succession is represented as being interrupted at regular intervals, and these interruptions are marked by small numbered letters representing the distinct forms known as varieties. But these interruptions could have been placed at any other points, if there had been sufficient time for the accumulation of a large amount of divergent variation.

title: On the Origin of Species
input: This passage summarizes the conditions that can influence natural selection, focusing on both favorable and unfavorable factors. It suggests that a large continental area, which is likely to experience significant fluctuations in elevation, is conducive to the emergence of diverse life forms that may thrive and expand over time. Initially, when this area exists as a continent, its diverse population will face intense competition. As subsidence transforms the continent into separate islands, many individuals of the same species will remain on each island, leading to restricted interbreeding at the edges of their ranges. This isolation, coupled with any physical changes, will hinder immigration, necessitating that new ecological niches be filled by adaptations of existing species. Over time, these modifications can lead to well-defined varieties. Should the islands eventually be uplifted back into a continental form, competition will resurge, allowing the more advantageous varieties to proliferate. This process may result in the extinction of less adapted forms, altering the relative proportions of the continent's inhabitants and providing further opportunities for natural selection to drive the evolution of new species.
human: To sum up the circumstances favourable and unfavourable to natural selection, as far as the extreme intricacy of the subject permits. I conclude, looking to the future, that for terrestrial productions a large continental area, which will probably undergo many oscillations of level, and which consequently will exist for long periods in a broken condition, will be the most favourable for the production of many new forms of life, likely to endure long and to spread widely. For the area will first have existed as a continent, and the inhabitants, at this period numerous in individuals and kinds, will have been subjected to very severe competition. When converted by subsidence into large separate islands, there will still exist many individuals of the same species on each island: intercrossing on the confines of the range of each species will thus be checked: after physical changes of any kind, immigration will be prevented, so that new places in the polity of each island will have to be filled up by modifications of the old inhabitants; and time will be allowed for the varieties in each to become well modified and perfected. When, by renewed elevation, the islands shall be re-converted into a continental area, there will again be severe competition: the most favoured or improved varieties will be enabled to spread: there will be much extinction of the less improved forms, and the relative proportional numbers of the various inhabitants of the renewed continent will again be changed; and again there will be a fair field for natural selection to improve still further the inhabitants, and thus produce new species.
base: This passage talks about what can affect natural selection, both good and bad things. A big land area that changes a lot in height is good for many different life forms to come up. When this area is a continent, the different animals and plants there have to compete a lot. But when the land goes down and becomes islands, the same species end up on each island. That means they can't mix much, so they have to adapt to their own environment. If the islands go back up into a continent, the competition comes back, and the best adapted ones survive. Over time, this can lead to new species. The less adapted ones might die out, changing the mix of life on the continent. That gives natural selection more chances to shape new species.
finetuned: I cannot here attempt to trace the whole series of conditions which may influence natural selection, but will merely recapitulate those which I believe to be most important. The most important of all, I think, is the large continental area, which is likely to be most affected by great fluctuations in the level of the land. This will be the seat of a vast number of diversified forms, which, in the course of time, may increase and multiply. When this area is a continent, its inhabitants will be in fierce competition; but when it has been subsided into several islands, many of the same species will be left on each, and these will be unable to interbreed with each other, or with any other individuals of the same species, at the edges of their range. They will thus be isolated from each other, and from any other individuals of the same species, by any physical change which may have occurred, and by any distance from the shores. Immigration will thus be prevented, and the new spaces must be filled by modifications of the same species. These modifications will be selected for and retained, and will become well-defined varieties. If the islands afterwards become raised into a continental form, competition will again be fierce; and the more vigorous and well-adapted varieties will again increase and multiply, while the less adapted will be exterminated, and the relative proportions of the inhabitants will have been altered. Natural selection will thus again have an opportunity of working.

title: On the Origin of Species
input: Natural selection may be a powerful process when compared to human selection, influencing traits that might seem trivial in importance. It appears to operate across various ages and can affect both males and females. Sexual selection also plays a role in this process. There tends to be a general tendency for interbreeding among individuals of the same species, which can be influenced by both favorable and unfavorable conditions for natural selection, including factors such as intercrossing, isolation, and population size. The effects of natural selection may often be slow and gradual, and it can lead to extinction in certain cases. The divergence of characteristics seems to be linked to the variety of organisms in small areas and the process of naturalization. Overall, the actions of natural selection through the divergence of traits and extinction contribute to the evolution of descendants from a shared ancestor, providing an explanation for the categorization of all living organisms.
human: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes. Sexual Selection. On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species. Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals. Slow action. Extinction caused by Natural Selection. Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation. Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent. Explains the Grouping of all organic beings.
base: Natural selection can be a strong force when compared to human choices, shaping traits that might seem unimportant. It works over many years and affects both men and women. Sexual selection is part of this too. Animals often mate with others of their kind, and this can be shaped by good or bad conditions, like how they crossbreed, how isolated they are, and how many there are. Natural selection can move slowly, and in some cases, it can cause species to go extinct. Differences between species seem to come from the many life forms in small areas and how they spread into new places. Overall, natural selection through these changes and extinctions helps explain how different life forms come from a common ancestor, which is why we group all living things into categories.
finetuned: Natural selection, as compared with man’s choice, is a powerful agent in the production of effects which might seem unimportant. It acts on all ages, on both sexes, and is aided by sexual selection. There is a general tendency to intercross, and the tendency is modified by the presence or absence of conditions which are favourable or unfavourable to natural selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, and the size of the population. The action of natural selection is slow and gradual, and sometimes fatal to the species, and causes the divergence of characteristics, which is the most important of all causes in the production of varieties. This divergence of characteristics, caused by the variety of organic beings in small areas and by the process of naturalization, is the great means of producing the descendants of a common progenitor, and explains all the classifications of the living and extinct inhabitants of the world.

title: On the Origin of Species
input: If species are considered to be distinct and stable varieties, it may be easier to understand why their hybrid offspring might exhibit similar complex patterns in terms of resemblance to their parents. This includes being blended through successive crossings and other related characteristics, much like the hybrid offspring of recognized varieties. Conversely, these observations could appear puzzling if species were created independently while varieties were formed through secondary processes. Ultimately, this raises important questions about the nature of species and varieties in the context of their relationships and origins.
human: If species be only well-marked and permanent varieties, we can at once see why their crossed offspring should follow the same complex laws in their degrees and kinds of resemblance to their parents, - in being absorbed into each other by successive crosses, and in other such points, - as do the crossed offspring of acknowledged varieties. On the other hand, these would be strange facts if species have been independently created, and varieties have been produced by secondary laws.
base: If species are seen as distinct and stable, it's easier to explain why their hybrids might show similar complex patterns like their parents. They can blend over many crossings and share other traits, just like hybrids between known varieties. But if species were created separately and varieties came from later changes, these observations might seem strange. This makes us think more about what species and varieties really are and how they relate to each other.
finetuned: If species were simply distinct and stable varieties, we might easily understand why their hybrids should be as complex in their resemblance to the parent-species as the hybrids of known varieties. They would be blended by successive crossings and other allied characters, as the hybrids of known varieties. But these facts would be puzzling, if species were created independently, and varieties formed by secondary laws.

title: Jane Eyre
input:
The door at the end of the gallery opened, revealing Mr. Rochester, who emerged with a candle in hand after coming down from the upper floor. One of the ladies quickly approached him and grasped his arm; it was Miss Ingram. 

He responded with a hint of humor, saying, “But please don’t pull me down or strangle me,” as the Misses Eshton began to cling to him as well. Meanwhile, the two older women, dressed in large white wraps, were making their way toward him with an air of urgency. 

He may have seemed somewhat imposing at that moment, with his dark eyes flashing. Taking a moment to compose himself, he continued.

He looked a little formidable, with his dark eyes blazing. He took a moment to recover himself, and then continued.

title: Jane Eyre
input:
I recalled everything quite clearly; the language, the look, and the tone felt momentarily refreshed. I found myself in the classroom where Adèle was drawing. I leaned over her to guide her pencil, and she glanced up, surprised. 

“What is it, Miss?” she asked. “Your fingers are trembling like a leaf, and your cheeks are red — so red, like cherries!” 

I quickly tried to push away the unpleasant thought I had been forming about Grace Poole; it was unsettling to me. When I compared myself to her, I noticed our differences. Bessie Leaven had mentioned that I was quite a lady, and there was truth to that—I recognized that I was indeed a lady. title: Pride and Prejudice
input: The speaker expresses a clear position on their feelings toward Mr. Wickham, stating that they are not in love with him at present. However, they acknowledge that he is the most charming person they have encountered. The speaker believes it may be beneficial if Mr. Wickham does not develop a strong attachment to them, recognizing the potential imprudence of such a situation. They mention their father's high regard for them, which they value greatly and would not want to jeopardize. Despite their father's favorable view of Mr. Wickham, the speaker emphasizes their concern about causing unhappiness for their family. They observe that young people often pursue romantic relationships despite financial constraints, raising questions about their own ability to resist temptation. Ultimately, they commit to taking their time and not rushing into conclusions about their feelings, stating their intention to remain composed and thoughtful in their interactions with Mr. Wickham.
human: “I beg your pardon. I will try again. At present I am not in love with Mr. Wickham; no, I certainly am not. But he is, beyond all comparison, the most agreeable man I ever saw - and if he becomes really attached to me - I believe it will be better that he should not. I see the imprudence of it. Oh, that abominable Mr. Darcy! My father’s opinion of me does me the greatest honour; and I should be miserable to forfeit it. My father, however, is partial to Mr. Wickham. In short, my dear aunt, I should be very sorry to be the means of making any of you unhappy; but since we see, every day, that where there is affection young people are seldom withheld, by immediate want of fortune, from entering into engagements with each other, how can I promise to be wiser than so many of my fellow-creatures, if I am tempted, or how am I even to know that it would be wiser to resist? All that I can promise you, therefore, is not to be in a hurry. I will not be in a hurry to believe myself his first object. When I am in company with him, I will not be wishing. In short, I will do my best.”

As Mr. Darcy approached, seemingly without any intention of engaging in conversation, Miss Lucas challenged her friend to bring up a particular topic. This prompted Elizabeth to address him directly, asking, “Did you think, Mr. Darcy, that I expressed myself particularly well just now when I was encouraging Colonel Forster to organize a ball at Meryton?” 

Mr. Darcy responded, noting, “You are quite an unusual friend, always wanting me to perform for everyone. If I were more vain about my musical abilities, you would be quite helpful; however, I would prefer not to perform in front of those who are accustomed to hearing the best.” Despite his reluctance, he acquiesced when Miss Lucas persisted, saying, “Very well; if it must be done, then it shall be.” He then looked at Mr. Darcy and referenced an old saying that everyone present would know, stating, “Keep your breath to cool your porridge,” and concluded that he would reserve his breath for singing.

title: Great Expectations
input:
Miss Havisham sat in silence, her head resting in her hands, making a low sound of distress while gently rocking in her chair, but she did not respond. 

"Or," Estella suggested, "if you had taught her, from the very beginning of her understanding, with all your strength and effort, that daylight existed, but that it was her adversary and could harm her, leading her to turn away from it because it had caused you pain and would likely do the same to her; if you had instilled this belief, and later wished for her to embrace the daylight naturally but she found it difficult to do so, you might have felt disappointed and upset, wouldn’t you?" 

In summary, the conversation reflects the complexities of expectations and the potential impact of early beliefs on an individual's relationship with the world.

title: The Federalist Papers
input: The observations discussed indicate that the composition of legislative bodies is primarily influenced by the interests and perspectives of various community classes. Regardless of whether representation is extensive or limited, it tends to consist predominantly of landowners, merchants, and professionals who effectively represent these diverse interests. While it may be noted that other types of individuals have been observed in local legislatures, these cases are exceptions and not numerous enough to significantly change the overall characteristics of the government. Strong individuals from all backgrounds can overcome challenges posed by their circumstances and gain recognition for their abilities, receiving respect from both their specific groups and society at large. Ideally, opportunities should be accessible to everyone. It is hoped that examples of notable individuals will emerge in both federal and state legislation. However, such instances do not undermine the reasoning based on the prevailing patterns observed.
human: WE HAVE seen that the result of the observations, to which the foregoing number has been principally devoted, is, that from the natural operation of the different interests and views of the various classes of the community, whether the representation of the people be more or less numerous, it will consist almost entirely of proprietors of land, of merchants, and of members of the learned professions, who will truly represent all those different interests and views. If it should be objected that we have seen other descriptions of men in the local legislatures, I answer that it is admitted there are exceptions to the rule, but not in sufficient number to influence the general complexion or character of the government. There are strong minds in every walk of life that will rise superior to the disadvantages of situation, and will command the tribute due to their merit, not only from the classes to which they particularly belong, but from the society in general. The door ought to be equally open to all; and I trust, for the credit of human nature, that we shall see examples of such vigorous plants flourishing in the soil of federal as well as of State legislation; but occasional instances of this sort will not render the reasoning founded upon the general course of things, less conclusive.
base: The observations show that who is in charge of making laws depends a lot on the interests and views of different groups in society. Whether the government has a lot of people or not, the main people in charge are usually landowners, business people, and professionals. These groups stand for different interests. Other people have been seen in local governments, but they are not common enough to change the main picture. Strong people from any background can still succeed and get respect from their own group and the whole society. Everyone should have a chance to be part of the government. It's hoped that there will be famous people in both national and state legislatures. But even if there are, it doesn't change the main idea we saw.
finetuned: The observations which I have been making upon this subject show me, that the composition of the legislative bodies, in all the countries which I have had the good fortune to visit, depends in a great measure on the interests and views of the different classes of the community. Whether it be an extensive or a limited representation, it is almost always composed of landholders, merchants, and professional men, who represent the various interests of the country. I may mention that other persons have been seen in the local legislatures, but these are exceptions, and not numerous enough to alter in the slightest degree the character of the government. Strong men, from every class of society, overcome the difficulties which their circumstances impose upon them, and are generally distinguished for their talents, and respected by their own class and the public at large. The opportunities should be equal to all. I wish to see some remarkable men in the federal and in the state legislatures. But such examples do not invalidate the reasoning which is founded upon the general laws of the case.

title: The Federalist Papers
input:
The importance of having a Constitution that is at least as effective as the one being proposed for maintaining the Union is the issue we are currently examining. 

This discussion may be divided into three main areas: the goals that the federal government should address, the amount of authority needed to achieve those goals, and the individuals who should be subject to that authority. The organization and distribution of this power will be more appropriately considered in the following section.
human:
THE necessity of a Constitution, at least equally energetic with the one proposed, to the preservation of the Union, is the point at the examination of which we are now arrived.

This inquiry will naturally divide itself into three branches - the objects to be provided for by the federal government, the quantity of power necessary to the accomplishment of those objects, the persons upon whom that power ought to operate. Its distribution and organization will more properly claim our attention under the succeeding head.

We’re looking at three main points: what the federal government should do, how much power it needs to do that, and who should be under that power. How that power is organized and shared will come up next.

In essence, if he were to proceed under this impression to examine the various State constitutions, he would undoubtedly experience great disappointment upon discovering that only two of them included a prohibition against standing armies in times of peace. The remaining eleven either remained completely silent on the issue or explicitly acknowledged the authority of the Legislature to permit their existence.

Moreover, he would still find it difficult to dismiss the notion that there must be some credible basis for the outcry regarding this matter. He would likely be unable to conceive, while any potential sources of information remained unexamined, that the issue was merely an attempt to manipulate public belief, either stemming from a calculated intention to mislead or from an excessive zeal that lacked sincerity. It may occur to him that he might discover the safeguards he sought within the original agreement among the States. At this point, he would anticipate finding a resolution to the puzzle. He would likely reason that the current Confederation must include the most definitive provisions against military establishments in times of peace and that a deviation from this principle, particularly in a favored aspect, has led to the discontent that seems to motivate these political advocates.

title: The Federalist Papers
input: Another resource for influencing how European nations act toward us in this area may come from establishing a federal navy. It seems likely that if the Union continues under an effective government, we would be in a position, before too long, to build a navy that, while it might not match those of the major maritime powers, could still carry respectable weight if added to the scale of either of two contending sides. This tends to be especially true with regard to operations in the West Indies. A few ships of the line, sent at the right time to reinforce either side, could often be enough to determine the outcome of a campaign, and matters of the greatest importance might depend on that outcome. Our position in this respect is a very strong one. If we also consider how useful supplies from this country can be in carrying out military operations in the West Indies, it can readily be seen that such a favorable situation would allow us to negotiate with considerable advantage for commercial privileges. A price could be placed not only on our friendship but also on our neutrality. By steadily adhering to the Union, we may hope before long to become the arbiter of Europe in America and to be able to tilt the balance of European rivalries in this part of the world as our interests may require.

title: Middlemarch
input: Upon returning home, Lydgate received a visit from Mr. Farebrother. The Vicar had not been in town the previous day, but news of an execution at Lydgate's residence reached Lowick by evening, carried by Mr. Spicer, the shoemaker and parish clerk, who learned it from his brother, a respected bell-hanger in Lowick Gate. Since the evening when Lydgate descended from the billiard room with Fred Vincy, Mr. Farebrother's thoughts about him had turned rather somber. While playing at the Green Dragon might seem trivial for another man, in Lydgate, it appeared to be one of several indicators that he was becoming different from his former self. He was starting to engage in activities that he had previously regarded with disdain. Although some whispers about dissatisfaction in Lydgate's marriage might have contributed to this change, Mr. Farebrother suspected that the primary issue was the growing reports of Lydgate's debts, leading him to worry that any belief in Lydgate's hidden resources or support could be misguided. The disappointment he had faced in his initial attempt to earn Lydgate's trust made him hesitant to try again, but the news of the execution taking place in the house prompted the Vicar to set aside his reluctance.

He was beginning to do things for which he had formerly even an excessive scorn. The rebuff he had met with in his first attempt to win Lydgate’s confidence, disinclined him to a second; but this news of the execution being actually in the house, determined the Vicar to overcome his reluctance.

title: Middlemarch
input: “I shall be exceedingly grateful if you would be willing to visit me here from time to time, Mr. Lydgate,” the banker remarked following a moment of contemplation. “If, as I cautiously anticipate, I am fortunate enough to have you as a valuable collaborator in the intriguing subject of hospital administration, there will be numerous matters that we must address in a confidential setting. Regarding the new hospital, which is nearly complete, I will reflect on your comments concerning the benefits of a specialized facility for treating fevers. The ultimate decision will be mine, as although Lord Medlicote has generously provided the land and timber for the construction, he is not inclined to dedicate his personal attention to this endeavor.”

As to the new hospital, which is nearly finished, I shall consider what you have said about the advantages of the special destination for fevers. The decision will rest with me, for though Lord Medlicote has given the land and timber for the building, he is not disposed to give his personal attention to the object.”

title: Common Sense
input: Some may argue that once relations with Britain are repaired, the country will provide protection. This raises the question of whether it is wise to suggest that Britain would maintain a navy in our ports for that purpose. Common sense indicates that a power that has sought to conquer us is not the most appropriate choice for our defense. This highlights the potential for conquest to occur under the guise of friendship, risking that, after a prolonged and courageous struggle, we could be deceived into a state of subjugation. If British ships are not allowed in our harbors, one might wonder how they could effectively safeguard us. A navy located three or four thousand miles away would have limited utility, particularly during urgent situations. Ultimately, if we must defend ourselves, it stands to reason that we should do so independently rather than relying on another nation.
human: Some, perhaps, will say, that after we have made it up with Britain, she will protect us. Can we be so unwise as to mean, that she shall keep a navy in our harbours for that purpose? Common sense will tell us, that the power which hath endeavoured to subdue us, is of all others, the most improper to defend us. Conquest may be effected under the pretence of friendship; and ourselves, after a long and brave resistance, be at last cheated into slavery. And if her ships are not to be admitted into our harbours, I would ask, how is she to protect us? A navy three or four thousand miles off can be of little use, and on sudden emergencies, none at all. Wherefore, if we must hereafter protect ourselves, why not do it for ourselves? Why do it for another?
base: Some may say that once relations with Britain are fixed, the country will protect us. But is it smart to claim Britain would keep a navy in our ports for that? Common sense says a power that tried to take over isn't the best for our safety. This shows how conquest could come in disguise of friendship, and we might end up in a bad situation after a long fight. If British ships aren't allowed in our ports, how can they really help us? A navy far away wouldn't be much use, especially when things get tight. So if we have to defend ourselves, it makes sense to do it on our own instead of depending on another country.
finetuned: “Some may perhaps say, that once we are reconciled with Britain, she will protect us; and to this it may be answered, that is it well to suggest that Britain will keep a navy in our ports for that purpose? A nation which has attempted to conquer us, is not the best friend to defend us. For it is not improbable, that, after a long and valiant resistance, we should be betrayed into a state of subjugation. If our harbors are not open to her ships, how will they protect us? A navy at three or four thousand miles distant, is of little use, in an emergency. And if we must defend ourselves, we must do it without the assistance of any other nation.”

title: Common Sense
input: The contest for the monarchy and succession, between the Houses of York and Lancaster, subjected England to a prolonged period of violence. Over the course of this conflict, twelve major battles, in addition to various skirmishes and sieges, were waged between Henry and Edward. On two occasions, Henry was taken captive by Edward, only to find himself in a similar position at the hands of Henry. Furthermore, the unpredictable nature of warfare and the sentiments of a nation are evident, particularly when personal disputes serve as the foundation for conflict. This is illustrated by the fact that Henry was triumphantly escorted from a prison to a palace, while Edward was compelled to flee from a palace to a foreign land. However, as is often the case with abrupt changes in fortune, such transitions are rarely enduring; thus, Henry was ultimately displaced from the throne, and Edward was reinstated to succeed him. It is worth noting that Parliament consistently aligned itself with the faction that appeared strongest.
human: The contest for monarchy and succession, between the houses of York and Lancaster, laid England in a scene of blood for many years. Twelve pitched battles, besides skirmishes and sieges, were fought between Henry and Edward. Twice was Henry prisoner to Edward, who in his turn was prisoner to Henry. And so uncertain is the fate of war and the temper of a nation, when nothing but personal matters are the ground of a quarrel, that Henry was taken in triumph from a prison to a palace, and Edward obliged to fly from a palace to a foreign land; yet, as sudden transitions of temper are seldom lasting, Henry in his turn was driven from the throne, and Edward recalled to succeed him. The parliament always following the strongest side.
base: The war between the York and Lancaster families for the throne kept England in a state of violence for a long time. During this time, Henry and Edward fought in twelve major battles, plus many smaller fights and sieges. Twice, Henry was captured by Edward, only to be captured again by Henry. The war was full of uncertainty, and people’s feelings often changed, especially when the conflict was based on personal disagreements. This is shown by the fact that Henry was taken from prison to a palace, while Edward had to leave a palace and go to another country. But as often happens when things change suddenly, those changes don’t last. In the end, Henry lost the throne and Edward took his place. It’s also important to remember that Parliament usually supported the group that seemed the strongest.

In the course of this contest, twelve great battles, besides several skirmishes and sieges, were fought between Henry and Edward. On two occasions, Henry was taken prisoner by Edward, only to be in like circumstances at the hands of Henry. The uncertainty of war, and the passions of a nation, are manifest, especially when the foundation of contention is a private quarrel. For instance, Henry was triumphantly carried from a prison to a palace; Edward was driven from a palace into a foreign country. But, as is usual in sudden changes of fortune, such changes seldom endure; Henry was thrown off the throne, and Edward was restored to succeed him. And Parliament always adhered to the party that seemed strongest.

title: Common Sense
input: Immediate necessity can render certain actions convenient, but if such actions continue unchecked, they may lead to oppression. It is important to distinguish between expedience and what is right. During the crises that America faced, the appointment of representatives from various Houses of Assembly was a practical and appropriate solution for consultation, and this approach helped to protect the continent from disaster. However, it is likely that a Congress will always be in existence, and it is essential for those invested in maintaining order to consider how its members are chosen. This raises a question for those who study human behavior: is it wise for a single group of individuals to hold both representation and election powers? As we plan for future generations, it is crucial to recognize that virtue is not something that can be inherited.
human: Immediate necessity makes many things convenient, which if continued would grow into oppressions. Expedience and right are different things. When the calamities of America required a consultation, there was no method so ready, or at that time so proper, as to appoint persons from the several Houses of Assembly for that purpose; and the wisdom with which they have proceeded hath preserved this continent from ruin. But as it is more than probable that we shall never be without a Congress, every well wisher to good order, must own, that the mode for choosing members of that body, deserves consideration. And I put it as a question to those, who make a study of mankind, whether representation and election is not too great a power for one and the same body of men to possess? When we are planning for posterity, we ought to remember, that virtue is not hereditary.
base: Immediate need can make some actions seem easy, but if they go on without check, they can become unfair. It’s key to tell the difference between what’s handy and what’s right. When America was in trouble, letting people from different groups pick leaders worked well and helped keep the country safe. But a Congress is probably always going to be there, so those who care about order must think about how its members are chosen. This brings up a question for those who study people: is it smart for one group to have both the power to choose and the power to represent? As we think about the future, we must remember that good character isn’t something you’re born with.
finetuned:
1. Expediency can make what is expedient convenient; but if it continues, it may make it oppressive. It is a distinction of great importance between what is expedient and what is right.

2. In the emergencies which America has sustained, it was a practical and proper expedient to consult the representatives of the several Houses of Assembly; and this expedient saved the continent from destruction.

3. A Congress is probably to be always in being; and those who concern themselves about the preservation of order, must consider how its members are chosen. It is a question which the philosophers of mankind are daily asking themselves, whether it is wise to confide the powers of representation and election to the same body of men. We are to provide for the future ages of our country; and to this end we must recollect, that virtue is not hereditary.

title: Common Sense
input:
It may be suggested that describing the constitution of England as a union of three powers that check each other may overlook some complexities, as this characterization might not fully capture the nuances involved. 

Firstly, it can often be argued that the monarchy may present a tendency towards seeking absolute power, which implies the necessity of oversight to ensure that such ambitions are kept in check. 

Secondly, there is a notion that the Commons, due to their appointment, may be viewed as more prudent or deserving of trust compared to the crown. 

In summary, the relationship among the powers within the English constitution is complex and may be subject to differing interpretations.
human:
To say that the constitution of England is a union of three powers reciprocally checking each other, is farcical, either the words have no meaning, or they are flat contradictions.

First. - That the king is not to be trusted without being looked after, or in other words, that a thirst for absolute power is the natural disease of monarchy.

Secondly. - That the commons, by being appointed for that purpose, are either wiser or more worthy of confidence than the crown.
base: The idea that the English constitution is a balance of three powers checking each other might miss some of the finer points. The monarchy could push for more power, so there needs to be a way to stop that. The Commons, because they’re chosen, might seem smarter or more trustworthy than the crown. The way the powers work in England is tricky and can be seen differently by people.
finetuned:
But if any one be disposed to contend, that to denominate the constitution of England a union of three powers, which have a due check on each other, is to give an erroneous idea of the matter, I shall not be so hardy as to dispute it.

It may be said, that the crown, by its nature, is apt to be desirous of absolute power; and that, therefore, there is a necessity of some check to prevent it from obtaining it.

Again, the commons, by their appointment, may be considered as more reasonable than the crown, and therefore more deserving of confidence.

title: Common Sense
input: Human beings may have started as equals in the process of creation, and this equality could only have been altered by later circumstances. The differences between wealth and poverty can often be explained, perhaps without needing to resort to the more severe terms of oppression and greed. While oppression can frequently be a result of wealth disparities, it is rarely the direct cause of them. Additionally, while greed may help someone avoid severe financial hardship, it often makes them too cautious to achieve true wealth. In summary, the dynamics of equality and wealth are complex and influenced by various factors.
human: Mankind being originally equals in the order of creation, the equality could only be destroyed by some subsequent circumstance; the distinctions of rich, and poor, may in a great measure be accounted for, and that without having recourse to the harsh ill sounding names of oppression and avarice. Oppression is often the consequence, but seldom or never the means of riches; and though avarice will preserve a man from being necessitously poor, it generally makes him too timorous to be wealthy.
base: We started off equal, created by the same hand. That equality changed over time, shaped by what came after. The gap between rich and poor isn’t always about bad things like being forced to suffer or wanting more than you need. Oppression might come from being poor, but it doesn’t start the gap. Greed can help someone stay out of trouble, but it stops them from really getting ahead. All of this makes the story of equality and money a mix of different things.
finetuned: Man began creation, as it is said, equal, and this equality was only changed by later circumstances. The inequality of wealth and of poverty is easily explained, perhaps, without needing to appeal to the harsher terms of oppression and greed. Where oppression is frequently the effect of inequality of wealth, it is seldom the cause; and where greed keeps down the poor from famine, it keeps them too cautious to be rich.

title: Emma
input:
Emma found herself somewhat entertained by the idea that it was quite unusual and felt she had no defense for him. 

“I really cannot understand,” Mrs. Elton remarked, feeling the slight as any wife might, “how he could possibly do such a thing to you, of all people! You are certainly the last person one would think could be overlooked! My dear Mr. E., I am confident he must have left a message for you. Not even Knightley could be that forgetful; it must be that his servants overlooked it. I think that is likely the situation, especially with the Donwell staff, who, as I have frequently noted, can be rather clumsy and forgetful. I certainly would not allow someone like his Harry to serve at our sideboard for any reason. And regarding Mrs. Hodges, Wright does not hold her in high regard at all. She promised him a receipt but failed to send it.” 

In summary, Mrs. Elton conveys her disbelief at the situation and expresses her confidence that a misunderstanding has occurred due to the negligence of others.

Depend upon it, that was the case: and very likely to happen with the Donwell servants, who are all, I have often observed, extremely awkward and remiss. - I am sure I would not have such a creature as his Harry stand at our sideboard for any consideration. And as for Mrs. Hodges, Wright holds her very cheap indeed. - She promised Wright a receipt, and never sent it.”

title: Emma
input: Mr. Weston's happiness was clear and unmistakable. He was truly delighted, as this was exactly the situation he had hoped for. Now Frank would genuinely be part of their neighborhood. After all, what did nine miles mean to a young man? Just an hour's ride. He would be able to visit constantly. The difference between Richmond and London in this regard was enough to determine whether they would see him regularly or not at all. Sixteen miles—or even eighteen, since it was a full eighteen to Manchester Street—was a serious obstacle. Even if he managed to get away, the entire day would be consumed by traveling there and back. There was no comfort in having him in London; he might as well be at Enscombe. Richmond, however, was exactly the right distance for easy visits. This suggests that closer was not necessarily better.

title: Emma
input: “A man,” he remarked, “must possess a significantly high opinion of himself when he invites others to leave the comfort of their own fireside to face a day such as this for the purpose of visiting him. He must believe himself to be a most agreeable individual; I could not undertake such an action. It is the utmost absurdity—indeed, it is presently snowing!—to insist that individuals forsake their comfort at home, as well as the folly of individuals not choosing to remain comfortably at home when they have the opportunity to do so. If we were compelled to venture out on an evening like this due to any obligation or necessity, we would consider it a considerable hardship; yet here we are, likely clad in somewhat lighter garments than usual, proceeding voluntarily, without justification, in defiance of the instinct of nature, which advises humanity, through every sensory experience, to remain at home and shelter what they can. title: Peter Pan
input:
After Mr. and Mrs. Darling departed the house, the night-lights beside the beds of the three children continued to glow brightly. They were particularly charming night-lights, and one might wish that the children could have stayed awake to see Peter. However, Wendy's light flickered and emitted a large yawn, which caused the other two lights to yawn as well. Before they could manage to stop, all three lights extinguished.

Now, a new light filled the room, a thousand times more brilliant than the night-lights. During the time it took to describe this, it had searched through all the drawers in the nursery, seeking Peter's shadow, rummaged through the wardrobe, and turned every pocket inside out. This was not a traditional light; it created illumination by moving rapidly. When it paused for a moment, one could see it was a fairy, no larger than a hand, yet still growing. Her name was Tinker Bell, and she was elegantly dressed in a skeleton leaf, tailored to showcase her figure effectively. She had a slight tendency toward being plump.

title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes

We heard the door open, followed by a brief conversation and rapid footsteps on the linoleum. Then, our own door opened and a woman, dressed in dark clothing and wearing a black veil, entered the room. This highlights the urgency of the situation. The woman was greeted warmly and offered refreshments, with the suggestion that she sit comfortably and share her story. It was also proposed that James be sent to bed, if that would be preferable. 

This suggests that the woman had spoken to us about her husband's issues before, seeking both medical and emotional support. As a doctor, I had previously discussed her husband's trouble with her, while my wife had offered comfort as an old friend and school companion. We responded with supportive words, attempting to soothe and comfort her. Ultimately, our conversation turned to the question of her husband's whereabouts and the possibility of his return. We asked if she knew where he was and whether it might be possible to bring him back to her.

He took a sovereign from his pocket and placed it on the table, turning away as if his discontent was too profound for expression. A few moments later, he paused under a lamp-post and laughed in a silent manner characteristic of him.

He noted that a man with distinctive whiskers and the "Pink ’un" newspaper visible from his pocket could easily be persuaded to share information through a wager. He suggested that if he had offered the man £100 directly, he would not have provided as thorough information as he did when prompted by the notion of a bet. Holmes then indicated that they were likely close to concluding their investigation, with only the decision remaining about whether to visit Mrs. Oakshott that evening or to postpone until the following day. He observed that the response from the unfriendly man implied that there were others, in addition to themselves, who were concerned about the situation.

title: Essays by Ralph Waldo Emerson
input: Additionally, human beings exhibit a propensity for timidity and apology, having abandoned an upright posture; they no longer dare to express their thoughts or assert their existence without referencing the opinions of revered individuals. Furthermore, they experience feelings of shame in the presence of even the most mundane aspects of the natural world, such as a blade of grass or a rose in bloom. It is worth noting that the roses situated beneath my window do not draw comparisons with previous or supposedly superior roses; instead, they exist solely for their present purpose, coexisting with a higher power in the current moment. Moreover, these roses are not bound by temporal constraints, for they are perfect and self-sufficient in every instant of their existence. In essence, the entire life cycle of a rose is inherently contained within each stage of its development, from the initial leaf-bud to the fully bloomed flower, and ultimately to the leafless root, with no aspect being more or less significant than any other. The nature of the rose is thus fulfilled, and it, in turn, fulfills the natural order, in a state of equilibrium that persists throughout all moments. However, human beings tend to postpone or reminisce, failing to live in the present, instead lamenting the past or anxiously anticipating the future, oblivious to the abundant resources that surround them. It is worth noting that humans cannot attain happiness and strength until they learn to coexist with nature in the present, transcending the limitations of time.
human: Man is timid and apologetic; he is no longer upright; he dares not say "I think," "I am," but quotes some saint or sage. He is ashamed before the blade of grass or the blowing rose. These roses under my window make no reference to former roses or to better ones; they are for what they are; they exist with God to-day. There is no time to them. There is simply the rose; it is perfect in every moment of its existence. Before a leaf-bud has burst, its whole life acts; in the full-blown flower there is no more; in the leafless root there is no less. Its nature is satisfied, and it satisfies nature, in all moments alike. But man postpones, or remembers; he does not live in the present, but with a reverted eye laments the past, or, heedless of the riches that surround him, stands on tiptoe to foresee the future. He cannot be happy and strong until he too lives with nature in the present, above time.

They no longer dare to speak their minds or declare their presence without referencing the views of those they hold in high regard. They feel ashamed even in the presence of simple natural things, like a blade of grass or a blooming rose. The roses under my window don’t compare to others; they exist only for now, living in the moment alongside a higher force. These roses are not bound by time, for they are perfect and complete in every moment. The entire life of a rose is contained in each stage, from the first leaf-bud to the full bloom, and then to the rootless leaf. No part is more important than another. The rose is complete, and in doing so, it fulfills the natural order, maintaining a balance that lasts always. Yet people tend to delay or dwell on the past, failing to live in the now. They mourn what was or fear what is to come, unaware of the abundance around them. Humans can never find true happiness and strength until they learn to live with nature in the present, beyond the limits of time.
