She took off the cap that had kept her hair bound. Her hair fell over her shoulders, dark and thick. The contrast of shadow and light softened her face. A gentle smile came to her lips and stayed in her eyes. It showed she was connected to her femininity. A warm color returned to her cheeks, which had been pale for a long time. Parts of her identity—her youth, her beauty—came back from what people thought was lost. They mixed with her hope and a new kind of happiness. The heavy feeling of the earth and sky faded along with their sorrow. Then, as if touched by a divine light, the sun broke through. It filled the dark forest with brightness. Every green leaf shimmered. The yellow leaves turned gold. The gray trees glowed. Things that had cast shadows now had light. The little brook’s path could be seen by the way it sparkled as it moved through the woods, now a place of joy.

title: The Scarlet Letter
input: The mariner informed Hester that he needed to arrange for an additional sleeping quarter beyond what had been agreed upon. He reassured her that there was no need for concern about scurvy or ship-related illnesses during the journey, as the presence of both a ship's surgeon and another doctor would mitigate health risks. He noted that the primary concern would be related to medications, especially since there was a significant supply of apothecary goods on board, which he had obtained through trade with a Spanish ship. Hester, taken aback by this news, asked for clarification, particularly regarding the possibility of an additional passenger.
human:
“So, mistress,” said the mariner, “I must bid the steward make ready one more berth than you bargained for! No fear of scurvy or ship-fever, this voyage! What with the ship’s surgeon and this other doctor, our only danger will be from drug or pill; more by token, as there is a lot of apothecary’s stuff aboard, which I traded for with a Spanish vessel.”

“What mean you?” inquired Hester, startled more than she permitted to appear. “Have you another passenger?”

title: The Scarlet Letter
input: On this particular day, there may have been an expression that had never been observed before or, indeed, one that was not easily recognizable now; unless perhaps there existed an extraordinarily perceptive observer who could first understand her heart and then look for a related change in her face and demeanor. Such a sensitive soul might have believed that after enduring the scrutinizing gaze of the crowd for seven long years—viewed as a necessity, a punishment, and something akin to a harsh faith—she now willingly faced it one last time, aiming to transform her prolonged suffering into a sense of triumph. She might have quietly addressed the onlookers, saying, “Take a good look at the scarlet letter and its bearer! Soon, she will be out of your reach! In just a few hours, the profound and mysterious ocean will extinguish and conceal forever the mark you have forced upon her.” It may not be too far-fetched to imagine that Hester felt a twinge of regret as she was on the verge of gaining her freedom from a pain that had become entwined with her very existence. Could she not have experienced an overwhelming urge to savor one final, intense taste of the bitter experiences that had flavored most of her adult life? The future may hold for her a life that is rich, delightful, and invigorating, served in a beautiful golden cup; otherwise, it might leave her with an unavoidable weariness following the bitterness that had long been her companion.

Might there not be an irresistible desire to quaff a last, long, breathless draught of the cup of wormwood and aloes, with which nearly all her years of womanhood had been perpetually flavored? The wine of life, henceforth to be presented to her lips, must be indeed rich, delicious, and exhilarating, in its chased and golden beaker; or else leave an inevitable and weary languor, after the lees of bitterness wherewith she had been drugged, as with a cordial of intensest potency.

title: The Scarlet Letter
input: He looked darkly at the clergyman and said that even if he had searched the whole earth, there was no place so secret, no high place or lowly place, where he could have escaped him, except on this very scaffold. Yet he trembled and turned to Hester with an expression of doubt and anxiety in his eyes. This was all the more evident because a feeble smile remained on his lips. Partly supported by Hester Prynne and holding one hand of little Pearl, the Reverend Mr. Dimmesdale turned to the dignified and venerable rulers, to the holy ministers who were his brethren, and to the people, whose great heart was thoroughly appalled yet overflowing with tearful sympathy. They knew that some deep life-matter, which if full of sin was full of anguish and repentance likewise, was now to be laid open to them. The sun, but little past its meridian, shone down upon the clergyman and gave a distinctness to his figure as he stood out from all the earth to put in his plea of guilty at the bar of Eternal Justice.

title: Moby Dick; Or, The Whale
input: When a Sperm Whale is captured in the Southern Fishery, it is generally not customary to begin the process of cutting it up immediately, especially late at night. This task is extremely labor-intensive, does not conclude quickly, and requires the full attention of the crew. Consequently, the typical practice is to take in all sail and secure the helm, allowing the crew to rest in their hammocks until dawn. However, two crew members must remain on deck in rotation for an hour at a time to monitor the situation, ensuring that everything proceeds smoothly until morning.
human: When in the Southern Fishery, a captured Sperm Whale, after long and weary toil, is brought alongside late at night, it is not, as a general thing at least, customary to proceed at once to the business of cutting him in. For that business is an exceedingly laborious one; is not very soon completed; and requires all hands to set about it. Therefore, the common usage is to take in all sail; lash the helm a’lee; and then send every one below to his hammock till daylight, with the reservation that, until that time, anchor-watches shall be kept; that is, two and two for an hour, each couple, the crew in rotation shall mount the deck to see that all goes well.
base: When a sperm whale is caught in the southern fishery, they don’t start cutting it right away, especially at night. It’s a lot of work, takes a long time, and needs everyone’s focus. So they take in all the sails and secure the wheel, let the crew rest in their hammocks until dawn. But two people have to stay on deck, taking turns every hour, to keep an eye on things and make sure everything goes smoothly until morning.
finetuned: When a Sperm Whale is hauled in the Southern Fishery, it is not customary to begin cutting her up, even at night, but the work is so tedious, so long, and requires so much attention, that all sail is taken in, and the helm is hove up, and the men are allowed to lie in hammocks till daylight; but two men are always kept on deck, in turn, an hour at a time, to watch, till all is well on deck, and everything is going smoothly, till morning.

title: Moby Dick; Or, The Whale
input: Meanwhile, while supervising another section of the vessel, Captain Peleg vociferously expressed his frustrations from the stern in an alarming manner. I nearly believed he might cause the ship to capsize prior to the retrieval of the anchor; consequently, I found myself pausing with my handspike and instructed Queequeg to do likewise, reflecting on the dangers we both faced in embarking on our journey under the command of such a volatile pilot. Despite this, I reassured myself with the notion that there might be some hope in the pious Bildad, notwithstanding his seven hundred seventy-seventh sermon. However, my thoughts were abruptly interrupted by a sudden and sharp impact to my rear, and upon turning, I was appalled to discover Captain Peleg in the process of retracting his leg from my immediate vicinity. That experience marked my first encounter with physical reprimand.
human: Meantime, overseeing the other part of the ship, Captain Peleg ripped and swore astern in the most frightful manner. I almost thought he would sink the ship before the anchor could be got up; involuntarily I paused on my handspike, and told Queequeg to do the same, thinking of the perils we both ran, in starting on the voyage with such a devil for a pilot. I was comforting myself, however, with the thought that in pious Bildad might be found some salvation, spite of his seven hundred and seventy-seventh lay; when I felt a sudden sharp poke in my rear, and turning round, was horrified at the apparition of Captain Peleg in the act of withdrawing his leg from my immediate vicinity. That was my first kick.

I almost thought he might actually do it, so I stopped holding my handspike and told Queequeg to do the same. I thought about how dangerous it was for both of us to be on a ship with such a temperamental captain. Still, I tried to believe there was some hope in Bildad, even with his seven hundred seventy-seventh sermon. But then I was hit hard in the back, and when I turned, I was shocked to see Captain Peleg pulling his leg back from where I was. That was the first time I ever got physically punished.

title: Moby Dick; Or, The Whale
input: As evening approached, I felt reasonably certain that all of his activities and rituals had concluded, so I decided to check on him in his room. I knocked gently on the door, but received no response. Attempting to open it, I found it securely fastened from within. "Queequeg," I called softly through the keyhole, but there was only silence. "I say, Queequeg! Why don’t you respond? It’s me—Ishmael." Yet, the stillness persisted, which began to concern me. I had given him ample time, and it crossed my mind that he may have experienced a medical issue. Peering through the keyhole, I was met with an odd angle, which provided a rather limited view. I could see only part of the bed frame and a section of the wall, with no further insight. It caught my attention to see Queequeg’s harpoon resting against the wall. The landlady had taken it from him the previous evening before we went to our room. This struck me as unusual, yet since the harpoon was indeed there and he rarely ventured out without it, it seemed likely he was still inside.

I tried to open it, but it was fastened inside. “Queequeg,” said I softly through the key-hole: - all silent. “I say, Queequeg! why don’t you speak? It’s I - Ishmael.” But all remained still as before. I began to grow alarmed. I had allowed him such abundant time; I thought he might have had an apoplectic fit. I looked through the key-hole; but the door opening into an odd corner of the room, the key-hole prospect was but a crooked and sinister one. I could only see part of the foot-board of the bed and a line of the wall, but nothing more. I was surprised to behold resting against the wall the wooden shaft of Queequeg’s harpoon, which the landlady the evening previous had taken from him, before our mounting to the chamber. That’s strange, thought I; but at any rate, since the harpoon stands yonder, and he seldom or never goes abroad without it, therefore he must be inside here, and no possible mistake.

title: Moby Dick; Or, The Whale
input: In essence, one must consider how, within this designated quest, Ahab fails to make contact with any land. Does his crew subsist solely on air? Surely, he must pause for water. However, this is not the case. For an extended period, the sun, akin to a circus performer, has traversed its fiery path, requiring no sustenance other than that which resides within itself. Thus, Ahab. Furthermore, it is important to observe the nature of the whaler. While other vessels are burdened with foreign goods destined for distant docks, the wandering whale ship carries only herself, her crew, their weapons, and their necessities. She contains the equivalent of an entire lake within her spacious hold. She is balanced with useful provisions rather than merely with unusable materials such as pig lead and kentledge. She retains years' worth of water. This water, sourced from the pristine wells of Nantucket, is preferred by the Nantucketer in the Pacific after three years at sea, over the brackish fluid acquired just the day before from the rivers of Peru or India. Thus, while other ships may have traveled from New York to China and back, stopping at numerous ports, the whale ship may not have encountered even a single grain of soil during that time; her crew having seen no one other than fellow sailors adrift like themselves. Consequently, if one were to inform them that another flood had occurred, they would merely respond, "Well, boys, here is the ark!"
human: But how now? in this zoned quest, does Ahab touch no land? does his crew drink air? Surely, he will stop for water. Nay. For a long time, now, the circus-running sun has raced within his fiery ring, and needs no sustenance but what’s in himself. So Ahab. Mark this, too, in the whaler. While other hulls are loaded down with alien stuff, to be transferred to foreign wharves; the world-wandering whale-ship carries no cargo but herself and crew, their weapons and their wants. She has a whole lake’s contents bottled in her ample hold. She is ballasted with utilities; not altogether with unusable pig-lead and kentledge. She carries years’ water in her. Clear old prime Nantucket water; which, when three years afloat, the Nantucketer, in the Pacific, prefers to drink before the brackish fluid, but yesterday rafted off in casks, from the Peruvian or Indian streams. Hence it is, that, while other ships may have gone to China from New York, and back again, touching at a score of ports, the whale-ship, in all that interval, may not have sighted one grain of soil; her crew having seen no man but floating seamen like themselves. So that did you carry them the news that another flood had come; they would only answer - “Well, boys, here’s the ark!”

input: This situation could not continue indefinitely; it seems unlikely that any horse could maintain its footing under such conditions, as the pain might be too significant. I tripped and fell rather hard on my knees. Smith was thrown off due to my fall, and given the speed at which I was moving, it is possible he landed quite forcefully. I managed to regain my feet and limped over to the edge of the road, where the ground was free of stones. The moon had just risen above the hedge, and in its light, I could see Smith lying a few yards away from me. He did not get up; he made a small attempt to do so but then let out a deep groan. I could have groaned as well, for I was experiencing considerable pain in both my foot and knees; however, horses tend to endure their discomfort quietly. I remained silent, standing still and listening. I heard another heavy groan from Smith; although he lay fully illuminated by the moon, I could not see any movement from him. Feeling helpless for both him and myself, I listened intently for the sound of a horse, wheels, or footsteps. The road was not heavily traveled, and at this hour, we might wait for quite some time before assistance arrived. I stood there, observing and listening. The night was calm and pleasant, with only the soft notes of a nightingale breaking the silence, and the only movement was from the white clouds near the moon and a brown owl that glided over the hedge. This scene reminded me of summer nights long ago, when I would lie beside my mother in the lovely green meadow at Farmer Grey's.

input: This highlights the importance of a gentle touch when handling horses, as it can contribute to their comfort, responsiveness, and overall temperament. Horses have sensitive mouths, which can respond to even the slightest adjustments made by the driver. When a horse's mouth has not been negatively affected by poor treatment, it can quickly understand the rider’s intentions. The speaker notes that their own mouth has remained unspoiled, which may explain the preference of their mistress over another horse named Ginger, despite Ginger's comparable abilities. Ginger often expressed frustration about her situation, attributing her less ideal mouth to the harsh training methods used in London. An older horse, Sir Oliver, reassured Ginger by pointing out that her strength and agility allowed her to carry a tall rider without needing to lower her head, suggesting that horses should accept their circumstances and remain willing as long as they are treated kindly.
human: Oh! if people knew what a comfort to horses a light hand is, and how it keeps a good mouth and a good temper, they surely would not chuck, and drag, and pull at the rein as they often do. Our mouths are so tender that where they have not been spoiled or hardened with bad or ignorant treatment, they feel the slightest movement of the driver's hand, and we know in an instant what is required of us. My mouth has never been spoiled, and I believe that was why the mistress preferred me to Ginger, although her paces were certainly quite as good. She used often to envy me, and said it was all the fault of breaking in, and the gag bit in London, that her mouth was not so perfect as mine; and then old Sir Oliver would say, “There, there! don't vex yourself; you have the greatest honor; a mare that can carry a tall man of our master's weight, with all your spring and sprightly action, does not need to hold her head down because she does not carry the lady; we horses must take things as they come, and always be contented and willing so long as we are kindly used.”

title: Black Beauty
input: Two days following the accident, Blantyre came to see me. He patted me and offered extensive praise. He informed Lord George that he believed the horse was aware of Annie's peril, just as he was. He stated, “I could not have controlled him even if I had wanted to; she should never ride another horse.” Through their discussion, I learned that my young mistress was now safe and would soon be able to ride again. This news brought me joy, and I began to anticipate a happy future.

This was good news to me and I looked forward to a happy life.

title: Black Beauty
input: Lady Harriet, who stayed at the hall, was often unwell and did not go out in the carriage. Lady Anne, on the other hand, tended to enjoy horseback riding with her brother or cousins. She was quite skilled at riding and was known to be cheerful and gentle, in addition to her beauty. She chose me as her horse and affectionately named me "Black Auster." I found these rides to be quite enjoyable, especially in the crisp, fresh air, sometimes accompanied by Ginger and at other times by Lizzie. Lizzie was a lively bay mare, almost thoroughbred, and was quite popular among the gentlemen due to her graceful movements and spirited nature. However, Ginger, who was more familiar with Lizzie, suggested that she could be somewhat anxious. Overall, these experiences tended to create a pleasant atmosphere for our rides.

title: Black Beauty
input: Jerry maintained an exceptionally clean environment for us and provided as much variety in our diet as he could, ensuring that we received an ample quantity of food. Furthermore, he consistently supplied us with an adequate amount of clean, fresh water, which he allowed to remain accessible to us both day and night, with the exception of moments when we returned from our labor in a warm state. It is worth noting that some individuals believe that a horse should not have unrestricted access to water; however, I have observed that when we are permitted to drink according to our needs, we tend to consume only small amounts at a time. This approach benefits us significantly more than consuming large quantities all at once, which typically occurs when we are deprived of water until we become thirsty and uncomfortable. Additionally, some grooms would return home to enjoy their beer, leaving us with nothing but dry hay and oats for hours, without any moisture to accompany them. Consequently, we would inevitably consume excessive amounts of water in a single instance, which could negatively affect our respiratory health and sometimes lead to stomach discomfort. In essence, one of the most valuable aspects of our time here was the respite we received on Sundays. We exerted considerable effort throughout the week, and I sincerely believe that we would have struggled to maintain our stamina without that day of rest. Moreover, it provided us with the opportunity to enjoy each other's company, during which time I learned about the history of my companion.
human: Jerry kept us very clean, and gave us as much change of food as he could, and always plenty of it; and not only that, but he always gave us plenty of clean fresh water, which he allowed to stand by us both night and day, except of course when we came in warm. Some people say that a horse ought not to drink all he likes; but I know if we are allowed to drink when we want it we drink only a little at a time, and it does us a great deal more good than swallowing down half a bucketful at a time, because we have been left without till we are thirsty and miserable. Some grooms will go home to their beer and leave us for hours with our dry hay and oats and nothing to moisten them; then of course we gulp down too much at once, which helps to spoil our breathing and sometimes chills our stomachs. But the best thing we had here was our Sundays for rest; we worked so hard in the week that I do not think we could have kept up to it but for that day; besides, we had then time to enjoy each other's company. It was on these days that I learned my companion's history.

That was better than drinking a lot at once when we were thirsty and uncomfortable. We worked hard all week, and I think we’d have trouble staying strong without that day off. Plus, it gave us a chance to spend time together, and during that time I found out about my friend’s past.

title: The Good Soldier
input: She had not spoken to Edward in many years; their conversations were limited to logistical matters such as train schedules and hiring staff. That afternoon, however, she felt compelled to confront him. He was precisely as she remembered. It was akin to reopening a book after ten years, only to find the text unchanged. His motives remained the same. He had refrained from discussing the case because he did not want her to tarnish her thoughts with the notion that a brother officer could engage in blackmail. He sought to protect the reputation of his former love. However, it was clear that she was not concerned for her husband. He insisted repeatedly that there was nothing else in the world that could be held against him. She did not believe his assurances.

title: The Good Soldier
input: This represents the saddest narrative I have ever encountered. My wife and I had been acquainted with the Ashburnhams for nine seasons in the town of Nauheim, cultivating a connection that was both intimate and characterized by a relaxed familiarity, akin to the relationship between a well-fitted glove and one’s hand. We were familiar with Captain and Mrs. Ashburnham to the extent that one could be acquainted with another individual; however, in a deeper sense, we were unaware of their true selves. It is worth noting that such a situation appears to be uniquely characteristic of English individuals. Until today, when I take the time to contemplate my understanding of this tragic situation, I must acknowledge that I knew virtually nothing about them. Moreover, six months prior, I had never visited England, and I certainly had not delved into the complexities of the English heart; my experiences had only skimmed the surface.
human: THIS is the saddest story I have ever heard. We had known the Ashburnhams for nine seasons of the town of Nauheim with an extreme intimacy - or, rather with an acquaintanceship as loose and easy and yet as close as a good glove's with your hand. My wife and I knew Captain and Mrs Ashburnham as well as it was possible to know anybody, and yet, in another sense, we knew nothing at all about them. This is, I believe, a state of things only possible with English people of whom, till today, when I sit down to puzzle out what I know of this sad affair, I knew nothing whatever. Six months ago I had never been to England, and, certainly, I had never sounded the depths of an English heart. I had known the shallows.

Even now, when I think about how little I knew about their tragedy, I realize I knew almost nothing. Six months before, I hadn’t even been to England, and I hadn’t really understood the English heart—just touched the surface.

input:
Mr. O’Connor had been hired by Tierney’s agent to campaign in one section of the ward. However, due to the unpleasant weather and his leaky boots, he spent much of the day by the fire in the Committee Room on Wicklow Street, accompanied by Jack, the elderly caretaker. They had been sitting there since darkness had fallen on the short October day. It was the sixth of October, and the outdoors was dreary and cold.

Mr. O’Connor tore a strip from the card and lit it to ignite his cigarette. As he did this, the flame illuminated a leaf of dark, glossy ivy tucked into the lapel of his coat. The old man observed him closely and then picked up the cardboard again, beginning to fan the fire gently while his companion smoked.

Delirium eventually subsides. He repeated her words, directing them inward: “What am I to do?” The instinct of the celibate urged him to restrain himself. However, the weight of his actions remained; even his sense of honor recognized that he needed to atone for this wrongdoing. 

As he sat beside her on the edge of the bed, Mary appeared at the door, informing him that the missus requested his presence in the parlour. He rose to don his coat and waistcoat, feeling more powerless than ever. Once he was dressed, he approached her to offer comfort. Everything would be fine, he assured her. He left her weeping on the bed, softly lamenting, “O my God!”

title: Leviathan
input: From this we may infer that when we believe any statement to be true, not because of the thing itself or because of principles of natural reason, but because of the authority and good opinion we have of the person who said it, then the speaker, or the person we believe in and trust, and whose word we accept, is the object of our faith, and the honor done in believing is done to that person alone. Consequently, when we believe that the Scriptures are the word of God, without having any immediate revelation from God himself, our belief, faith, and trust is in the Church, whose word we accept and rest upon. And those who believe what a prophet relates to them in the name of God accept the word of the prophet, do honor to him, and trust and believe in him regarding the truth of what he relates, whether he is a true prophet or a false one. And so it is also with all other history. For if I should not believe all that is written by historians about the glorious acts of Alexander or Caesar, I do not think the ghost of Alexander or Caesar would have any just cause to be offended, or anyone else except the historian. If Livy says the gods once made a cow speak, and we do not believe it, we do not distrust God in that, but Livy. So it is evident that whatever we believe on no other reason than what is drawn from the authority of men alone and their writings, whether they are sent from God or not, is faith in men only.

title: Leviathan
input: This highlights that even when individuals are willing to adhere to laws, disputes regarding a person's actions can still arise. These disputes can be categorized into two main questions: first, whether an action was taken or not; and second, if an action was taken, whether it was in accordance with the law or not. The first type is referred to as a question of fact, while the second is identified as a question of right. Consequently, unless the parties involved agree to accept the decision of a third party, known as an arbitrator, they remain in a state of conflict. Ultimately, it is a principle of natural law that those in dispute should submit their rights to the judgment of an arbitrator.
human: And because, though men be never so willing to observe these Lawes, there may neverthelesse arise questions concerning a mans action; First, whether it were done, or not done; Secondly (if done) whether against the Law, or not against the Law; the former whereof, is called a question Of Fact; the later a question Of Right; therefore unlesse the parties to the question, Covenant mutually to stand to the sentence of another, they are as farre from Peace as ever. This other, to whose Sentence they submit, is called an ARBITRATOR. And therefore it is of the Law of Nature, "That they that are at controversie, submit their Right to the judgement of an Arbitrator."

The other is whether what they did was allowed by the law. The first is a question of fact. The second is a question of right. Unless the people involved agree to let someone else, called an arbitrator, decide, they stay in conflict. Naturally, the idea is that those who are arguing should let an arbitrator decide their rights.

And unless they submit to the decision of an arbitrator, or third person, they are in a state of controversy. And it is the law of nature that those who are in controversy should submit their right to the judgment of an arbitrator.

Additionally, when individuals are regarded as possessing their own inherent characteristics, they are referred to as natural persons. Furthermore, when they are considered to be representing the words and actions of another entity, they are deemed to be artificial or feigned persons. 

In essence, the term "person" originates from the Latin language, whereas the Greeks utilize the term "prosopon," which denotes the face or outward appearance of an individual, often in the context of theatrical performances. Moreover, the Latin term "persona" signifies the disguise or outward appearance of a person, frequently in the form of a mask or visard, which is used to conceal one's identity on stage. It is worth noting that this concept has been extended to encompass any representative of speech and action, whether in tribunals or theaters. 

Moreover, a person can be considered equivalent to an actor, both in theatrical settings and in everyday conversation. Additionally, to personate means to act or represent oneself or another individual, and the person who assumes the role of another is said to bear their person or act in their name. Furthermore, this concept is exemplified in the words of Cicero, who states that he bears three persons: his own, that of his adversary, and that of the judge. It is worth noting that this representative can be referred to by various designations, including representer, representative, lieutenant, vicar, attorney, deputy, procurator, actor, and other similar terms.

When they are considered as his owne, then is he called a Naturall Person: And when they are considered as representing the words and actions of an other, then is he a Feigned or Artificiall person.

The word Person is latine: instead whereof the Greeks have Prosopon, which signifies the Face, as Persona in latine signifies the Disguise, or Outward Appearance of a man, counterfeited on the Stage; and somtimes more particularly that part of it, which disguiseth the face, as a Mask or Visard: And from the Stage, hath been translated to any Representer of speech and action, as well in Tribunalls, as Theaters. So that a Person, is the same that an Actor is, both on the Stage and in common Conversation; and to Personate, is to Act, or Represent himselfe, or an other; and he that acteth another, is said to beare his Person, or act in his name; (in which sence Cicero useth it where he saies, "Unus Sustineo Tres Personas; Mei, Adversarii, & Judicis, I beare three Persons; my own, my Adversaries, and the Judges;") and is called in diverse occasions, diversly; as a Representer, or Representative, a Lieutenant, a Vicar, an Attorney, a Deputy, a Procurator, an Actor, and the like.

When someone is seen as having their own traits, they're called natural persons. But if they're acting on behalf of another, they're called artificial or feigned persons. 

The word "person" comes from Latin. The Greeks used "prosopon," which means face or appearance, often in plays. The Latin "persona" means a mask or disguise, used to hide identity on stage. This idea has grown to include anyone who represents speech or action, whether in court or theater.

A person can also be like an actor, both on stage and in daily talk. To personate is to act for yourself or someone else. The person playing another is said to bear their person or act in their name. Cicero once said he has three persons: his own, his opponent's, and the judge's. This role can be called many things—representer, representative, lieutenant, vicar, attorney, deputy, procurator, actor, and more.

title: Leviathan
input: When the representative is a single individual, if he borrows money or incurs a debt through a contract, he alone bears responsibility; the other members do not share this liability. If the entity of the political body is embodied in one person who borrows money from an outsider—specifically, an individual who is not part of the same body—then the debt is solely that of the representative. This is because, should he possess authority through formal documentation to compel the members to repay what he has borrowed, he would consequently hold sovereignty over them. Therefore, such a grant would be void, as it stems from an error typically associated with human nature, and is an insufficient indication of the grantor's intent. Conversely, if the authority is acknowledged, the representative becomes sovereign, thereby falling outside the current discussion, which pertains solely to subordinate bodies. Consequently, no member is obligated to repay the borrowed debt; the responsibility rests solely with the representative. The lender, being an outsider to the formal documentation and the qualifications of the body, recognizes only those individuals who are engaged as debtors. Since the representative is capable of binding himself alone, he is the only debtor in this instance, and he must therefore repay the lender either from the common fund, if available, or from his own personal assets.
human: When The Representative Is One Man, If He Borrow Mony, Or Owe It, By Contract; He Is Lyable Onely, The Members Not If the person of the Body Politique being in one man, borrow mony of a stranger, that is, of one that is not of the same Body, (for no Letters need limit borrowing, seeing it is left to mens own inclinations to limit lending) the debt is the Representatives. For if he should have Authority from his Letters, to make the members pay what he borroweth, he should have by consequence the Soveraignty of them; and therefore the grant were either voyd, as proceeding from Errour, commonly incident to humane Nature, and an unsufficient signe of the will of the Granter; or if it be avowed by him, then is the Representer Soveraign, and falleth not under the present question, which is onely of Bodies subordinate. No member therefore is obliged to pay the debt so borrowed, but the Representative himselfe: because he that lendeth it, being a stranger to the Letters, and to the qualification of the Body, understandeth those onely for his debtors, that are engaged; and seeing the Representer can ingage himselfe, and none else, has him onely for Debtor; who must therefore pay him, out of the common stock (if there be any), or (if there be none) out of his own estate.
base: When a representative is a single person, if he borrows money or takes on a debt through a contract, he is the only one responsible. The others aren’t liable. If the political body is represented by one person who borrows from someone outside the body, the debt is just his. Why? Because if he had the power to make the others pay, he’d be in charge. That wouldn’t work. So the grant of power is wrong, a mistake people often make. It doesn’t show the right intent. But if the power is real, the representative is in charge, and this isn’t about them. So no one else has to pay. The debt is on the representative. The lender doesn’t know the body’s rules. He only sees the person who borrowed. Since the representative can take on the debt alone, he’s the only one who needs to pay. He can use the group’s money if it’s there, or his own.

If the person of the body politic is in one man, who borrows money of an alien, that is to say, of a man not of the same body, then the debt is that of the representative alone. Because, if he had authority by deed to make the members pay what he has borrowed, he would thereby have sovereignty over them; and such a grant is void, because it proceeds from a mistake, which is the nature of mankind, and is not a sufficient proof of the grantor’s intent. If, on the contrary, the authority is admitted, the representative is sovereign, and is out of the present discourse, which is only of subordinate bodies. Therefore no member is to pay the borrowed debt; but the representative alone. The lender is an alien to the deed and qualifications of the body; and knows only such men as are debtors. Since the representative can bind himself alone, he is the only debtor, and must pay either out of the common stock, if there be any, or out of his own estate.

title: The Wealth of Nations
input: If a guinea is the weekly pension of an individual, that person can use it to purchase a specific amount of necessities, comforts, and entertainment throughout the week. The extent of these purchases reflects the individual's actual wealth and their true weekly income. This income does not equate to both the guinea and the items it can buy; rather, it aligns more closely with one of these values. It is more accurate to consider the value of the goods purchased rather than the mere presence of the guinea itself.
human: Thus, if a guinea be the weekly pension of a particular person, he can in the course of the week purchase with it a certain quantity of subsistence, conveniencies, and amusements. In proportion as this quantity is great or small, so are his real riches, his real weekly revenue. His weekly revenue is certainly not equal both to the guinea and to what can be purchased with it, but only to one or other of those two equal values, and to the latter more properly than to the former, to the guinea’s worth rather than to the guinea.
base: A guinea is the weekly pension given to an individual. With that amount, the person can buy a certain amount of food, comfort, and entertainment for the week. How much they can spend shows their real wealth and how much they actually earn each week. The guinea itself isn’t the same as the things it can buy. It’s better to look at what the money can purchase rather than just the guinea.
finetuned: If a guinea is the weekly pension of an individual, he will use it to buy a certain quantity of necessaries, comforts, and amusements for the week; and the quantity of these, which he buys, is an exact measure of his real wealth and his real weekly revenue. It is not the guinea, and the goods which it will buy, that his weekly revenue is equal to, but it is one of these only. It is the value of the goods which he buys, and not the mere existence of the guinea.

title: The Wealth of Nations
input: It is worth noting that there exist two scenarios in which it is generally beneficial to impose certain burdens on foreign goods to promote domestic industry. Additionally, there are two further situations in which it may warrant careful consideration: the first pertains to the extent to which it is appropriate to maintain the unrestricted importation of specific foreign goods, while the second concerns the degree and manner in which it may be suitable to reinstate such unrestricted importation after it has been temporarily suspended.
human: As there are two cases in which it will generally be advantageous to lay some burden upon foreign for the encouragement of domestic industry, so there are two others in which it may sometimes be a matter of deliberation, in the one, how far it is proper to continue the free importation of certain foreign goods; and, in the other, how far, or in what manner, it may be proper to restore that free importation, after it has been for some time interrupted.

Then there are two more situations that need thought: one is whether it's right to keep bringing in certain foreign goods without limits, and the other is how and how much to bring them back once they've been stopped temporarily.

title: The Wealth of Nations
input: Moreover, although North America has not yet attained the same level of wealth as England, it is experiencing more rapid growth and is advancing at a greater pace towards further wealth acquisition. Additionally, the most significant indicator of a country's prosperity is the increase in its population. In essence, in Great Britain and most other European countries, the population is not expected to double in less than five hundred years. Furthermore, in the British colonies in North America, it has been observed that the population doubles in a significantly shorter period, typically ranging from twenty to twenty-five years. It is worth noting that this increase is no longer primarily attributed to the continuous influx of new inhabitants, but rather to the substantial multiplication of the population. Moreover, individuals who live to an advanced age often witness a large number of descendants from their own family, frequently ranging from fifty to a hundred, and sometimes exceeding this number. Labour is rewarded to such an extent that a large family, instead of being a burden, constitutes a source of wealth and prosperity for the parents. In fact, the labour of each child, prior to leaving their household, is estimated to yield a clear gain of approximately one hundred pounds to their parents. Additionally, a young widow with several young children, who would have limited prospects for remarriage among the middle or lower classes in Europe, is often courted as a desirable partner in North America. The value placed on children serves as a significant incentive for marriage, and it is therefore not surprising that the population in North America tends to marry at a relatively young age. Nevertheless, despite the substantial increase resulting from these early marriages, there is a persistent complaint regarding the scarcity of labour in North America. Moreover, the demand for labourers, as well as the resources allocated for their maintenance, appears to be increasing at a faster rate than the available labour force.
human: But though North America is not yet so rich as England, it is much more thriving, and advancing with much greater rapidity to the further acquisition of riches. The most decisive mark of the prosperity of any country is the increase of the number of its inhabitants. In Great Britain, and most other European countries, they are not supposed to double in less than five hundred years. In the British colonies in North America, it has been found that they double in twenty or five-and-twenty years. Nor in the present times is this increase principally owing to the continual importation of new inhabitants, but to the great multiplication of the species. Those who live to old age, it is said, frequently see there from fifty to a hundred, and sometimes many more, descendants from their own body. Labour is there so well rewarded, that a numerous family of children, instead of being a burden, is a source of opulence and prosperity to the parents. The labour of each child, before it can leave their house, is computed to be worth a hundred pounds clear gain to them. A young widow with four or five young children, who, among the middling or inferior ranks of people in Europe, would have so little chance for a second husband, is there frequently courted as a sort of fortune. The value of children is the greatest of all encouragements to marriage. We cannot, therefore, wonder that the people in North America should generally marry very young. Notwithstanding the great increase occasioned by such early marriages, there is a continual complaint of the scarcity of hands in North America. The demand for labourers, the funds destined for maintaining them increase, it seems, still faster than they can find labourers to employ.

title: The Wealth of Nations
input: The price of metals, particularly the precious ones, at the most productive mines worldwide, can have a significant impact on their price at other mines. For instance, the price of copper in Japan may influence its price at European copper mines. Similarly, the price of silver in Peru, or the amount of labour or goods it can purchase, tends to affect its price not only at European silver mines but also at those in China. Historically, after the discovery of Peruvian mines, many European silver mines were abandoned, as the value of silver decreased to the point where the cost of operating them could no longer be covered, and the expenses, including food, clothing, and lodging, could not be recouped with a profit. This scenario also played out in the mines of Cuba, St. Domingo, and even the original Peruvian mines after the discovery of the Potosi mines. Generally, the price of metals at most mines is influenced by the price at the most productive mine currently in operation, which means that, at many mines, the revenue can often barely cover the expenses of extraction and may not generate a substantial rent for the landlord. As a result, rent typically appears to account for a relatively small portion of the price of both coarse and precious metals, with labour and profit usually making up the larger share, and overall, the prices of metals are shaped by a combination of these factors.
human: The price, therefore, of the coarse, and still more that of the precious metals, at the most fertile mines in the world, must necessarily more or less affect their price at every other in it. The price of copper in Japan must have some influence upon its price at the copper mines in Europe. The price of silver in Peru, or the quantity either of labour or of other goods which it will purchase there, must have some influence on its price, not only at the silver mines of Europe, but at those of China. After the discovery of the mines of Peru, the silver mines of Europe were, the greater part of them, abandoned. The value of silver was so much reduced, that their produce could no longer pay the expense of working them, or replace, with a profit, the food, clothes, lodging, and other necessaries which were consumed in that operation. This was the case, too, with the mines of Cuba and St. Domingo, and even with the ancient mines of Peru, after the discovery of those of Potosi. The price of every metal, at every mine, therefore, being regulated in some measure by its price at the most fertile mine in the world that is actually wrought, it can, at the greater part of mines, do very little more than pay the expense of working, and can seldom afford a very high rent to the landlord. Rent accordingly, seems at the greater part of mines to have but a small share in the price of the coarse, and a still smaller in that of the precious metals. Labour and profit make up the greater part of both.

For example, the price of copper in Japan might influence the price at European copper mines. The price of silver in Peru, or how much labor or goods it can buy, affects not just European silver mines but also those in China. When Peruvian mines were discovered, many European silver mines closed because the value of silver dropped so much that the costs of running them couldn’t be covered. The same happened in Cuba, St. Domingo, and even the original Peruvian mines after Potosi was found. Usually, the price of metals at most mines is set by the price at the most productive mine still working. This means that at many mines, the money made often just covers the cost of digging and doesn’t leave much for the landowner. So, rent is usually a small part of the price of both common and precious metals. Labor and profit take up more of the price, and overall, metal prices come from all these things working together.

Thus, the price of copper at Japan is the price at all European copper mines; the price of silver at Peru, or the quantity of labour or goods it can purchase, is the price at all European silver mines, and also the price at all Chinese silver mines. After the discovery of the Peruvian mines, I believe that many European silver mines were deserted, because the price of silver was so low that the expense of running them could not be defrayed, and the expense of food, clothing, and lodging could not be recovered with profit. The same thing happened in the mines of Cuba, St. Domingo, and even in the original Peruvian mines after the discovery of the Potosi mines. In general, the price of metals at most mines is the price at the most productive mine in operation. Hence, in the mines where the price is so low, the revenue is but barely sufficient to pay the expense of extraction; and there is but little rent for the landlord. Hence, it appears that rent accounts for but a small part of the price of both the coarse and the precious metals, and that, in the former, labour and profit, and in the latter, perhaps, the same, form the larger part; and that the prices of metals, in general, are the effect of these three causes.

title: Dracula
input: The group proceeded to the back of the house, where they encountered a kitchen window. The Professor retrieved a small surgical saw from his case and handed it to a companion, indicating the iron bars protecting the window. The bars were cut through quickly, and using a long, thin knife, they managed to push back the sash fastening and open the window. The Professor entered first, followed by his companion. They observed that the kitchen and nearby servants' quarters were unoccupied. As they explored further, they discovered four servant-women lying on the dining-room floor, illuminated only by faint light filtering through the shutters. Their heavy breathing and the strong smell of laudanum indicated they were in a compromised state. The Professor and his companion exchanged glances, and he noted that they would address the women later. They then ascended to Lucy’s room. Briefly pausing at the door to listen for any sounds, they heard nothing and with anxious expressions, they gently opened the door and entered the room.

The Professor took a small surgical saw from his case, and handing it to me, pointed to the iron bars which guarded the window. I attacked them at once and had very soon cut through three of them. Then with a long, thin knife we pushed back the fastening of the sashes and opened the window. I helped the Professor in, and followed him. There was no one in the kitchen or in the servants’ rooms, which were close at hand. We tried all the rooms as we went along, and in the dining-room, dimly lit by rays of light through the shutters, found four servant-women lying on the floor. There was no need to think them dead, for their stertorous breathing and the acrid smell of laudanum in the room left no doubt as to their condition. Van Helsing and I looked at each other, and as we moved away he said: “We can attend to them later.” Then we ascended to Lucy’s room. For an instant or two we paused at the door to listen, but there was no sound that we could hear. With white faces and trembling hands, we opened the door gently, and entered the room.

They went up to Lucy’s room. They stopped at the door to listen, but there was nothing. With worried looks, they opened the door and went in.

They paused a moment at the door, listened, and heard nothing. Then with anxious looks they opened it gently and went in.

title: Dracula
input:
After some time, I left him. The attendant informs me that he remained quiet until just before dawn, when he began to grow uneasy and eventually became violent. This continued until he fell into a paroxysm that exhausted him to the point of fainting into a sort of coma.

For three nights, the same pattern has occurred: violent throughout the day, then quiet from moonrise to sunrise. I wish I could find some clue as to the cause. It would almost seem as though some influence comes and goes. A fortunate idea has occurred to me. Tonight we shall pit sane minds against mad ones. He escaped before without our assistance; tonight he shall escape with it. We shall give him an opportunity, and have the men ready to follow in case they are needed.

title: Dracula
input: A sound stirred me awake, perhaps the distant, sorrowful howling of dogs coming from far below in the valley, which I could not see. The sound seemed to resonate in my ears, and the dust particles around me appeared to shift shapes in response to it as they moved in the moonlight. I felt a struggle within me, as if my instincts—or perhaps my very essence—were trying to respond to this call. It was as though I were becoming entranced. The dust danced more rapidly, and the moonlight appeared to tremble as it passed through the surrounding darkness. Gradually, these lights formed vague, ghostly figures. Suddenly, I felt fully alert and bolted from the area, crying out in fear. The shapes that emerged from the moonlight were those of three spectral women, a haunting presence that I was destined to encounter. I sought refuge in my room, where the brightness of the lamp provided a sense of comfort, free from the moon’s eerie glow.
human: Something made me start up, a low, piteous howling of dogs somewhere far below in the valley, which was hidden from my sight. Louder it seemed to ring in my ears, and the floating motes of dust to take new shapes to the sound as they danced in the moonlight. I felt myself struggling to awake to some call of my instincts; nay, my very soul was struggling, and my half-remembered sensibilities were striving to answer the call. I was becoming hypnotised! Quicker and quicker danced the dust; the moonbeams seemed to quiver as they went by me into the mass of gloom beyond. More and more they gathered till they seemed to take dim phantom shapes. And then I started, broad awake and in full possession of my senses, and ran screaming from the place. The phantom shapes, which were becoming gradually materialised from the moonbeams, were those of the three ghostly women to whom I was doomed. I fled, and felt somewhat safer in my own room, where there was no moonlight and where the lamp was burning brightly.
base: A sound woke me, maybe the far-off, sad whine of dogs from below, where I couldn’t see. The noise echoed in my ears, and the dust around me seemed to twist as it moved in the moonlight. I felt a pull inside, like my instincts or my soul were trying to answer the call. It was as if I was being drawn in. The dust spun faster, and the moonlight flickered as it passed through the dark. Slowly, the light made shapes, ghostly and unclear. Then I snapped awake, scared, and ran into my room. The lamp’s light felt safe, keeping me away from the moon’s cold shine.

The dust seemed to shift itself as it moved, and to form new shapes in response to it, under the moonlight. I fought against it. My instincts, or my very soul, struggled to answer. I was half enchanted. The dust flew faster, and the moonlight trembled as it passed through the darkness. Then these lights formed vague, ghostly shapes. Then I was suddenly awake and rushed from the place, screaming. These shapes were those of three ghostly women. I was doomed to see them. I fled to my room, where the brightness of the lamp was a comfort, and the moonlight was unknown.

title: Dracula
input: I took his hand and made a promise to him. As he departed, I held my door open and watched him enter his room and close the door behind him. Meanwhile, I remained stationary and observed one of the maids walking quietly down the passage. She had her back turned towards me, and therefore did not notice my presence, and she proceeded to enter the room where Lucy was lying. This sight had a profound effect on me. Generally, devotion is a rare quality, and we are typically grateful to individuals who demonstrate it spontaneously to those we care about. In this instance, a young woman was setting aside her natural fears of death to sit vigil alone by the side of her beloved mistress, ensuring that the deceased would not be left unattended until she was laid to rest.
human: I took his hand, and promised him. I held my door open as he went away, and watched him go into his room and close the door. As I stood without moving, I saw one of the maids pass silently along the passage - she had her back towards me, so did not see me - and go into the room where Lucy lay. The sight touched me. Devotion is so rare, and we are so grateful to those who show it unasked to those we love. Here was a poor girl putting aside the terrors which she naturally had of death to go watch alone by the bier of the mistress whom she loved, so that the poor clay might not be lonely till laid to eternal rest....

At the same time, I stayed put and saw one of the maids walk quietly down the hallway. She turned away from me, so she didn't notice me, and went into the room where Lucy was lying. That scene hit me hard. Devotion is a rare thing, and we usually feel thankful when someone shows it naturally to the people we care about. But here, a young woman was putting aside her fear of death to sit by herself at her beloved mistress's side, making sure the dead wouldn't be left alone until she was buried.

title: Dracula
input: On May 18, the individual revisited the room during daylight to seek clarity about the situation. Upon reaching the doorway at the top of the stairs, they discovered that the door was closed and had been forcefully pushed against the frame, resulting in splintered woodwork. It was noted that the lock bolt had not been engaged, indicating that the door was secured from the inside. This suggests that the previous experience was not merely a dream, prompting the individual to consider taking action based on this assumption.
human: 18 May. - I have been down to look at that room again in daylight, for I must know the truth. When I got to the doorway at the top of the stairs I found it closed. It had been so forcibly driven against the jamb that part of the woodwork was splintered. I could see that the bolt of the lock had not been shot, but the door is fastened from the inside. I fear it was no dream, and must act on this surmise.

I reached the top of the stairs, and found the door closed and pushed against the frame, the splintered woodwork being a good deal broken. The lock bolt was not set, and it was closed from within. So it was not a dream. I thought it was a dream, but I did not believe it.

title: On Liberty
input: The concentration of all significant talent within the governing body can ultimately hinder its mental activity and capacity for progress. As a collective entity, the officials operate within a system that relies heavily on established rules, which can lead to complacency and habitual routines. When they do deviate from this routine, it often results in unexamined ideas influenced by prominent individuals within the group. The only effective way to counterbalance these opposing tendencies—complacency and impulsive ideas—is through the scrutiny of equally capable individuals outside the governing body. This highlights the necessity for independent avenues to cultivate talent and provide the experiences needed for sound judgment in practical matters. To ensure a proficient and innovative group of officials, it is crucial that not all tasks that nurture the skills needed for governance are monopolized by the governing body. This approach helps prevent the decline of the bureaucracy into a mere adherence to outdated practices.
human: It is not, also, to be forgotten, that the absorption of all the principal ability of the country into the governing body is fatal, sooner or later, to the mental activity and progressiveness of the body itself. Banded together as they are - working a system which, like all systems, necessarily proceeds in a great measure by fixed rules - the official body are under the constant temptation of sinking into indolent routine, or, if they now and then desert that mill-horse round, of rushing into some half-examined crudity which has struck the fancy of some leading member of the corps: and the sole check to these closely allied, though seemingly opposite, tendencies, the only stimulus which can keep the ability of the body itself up to a high standard, is liability to the watchful criticism of equal ability outside the body. It is indispensable, therefore, that the means should exist, independently of the government, of forming such ability, and furnishing it with the opportunities and experience necessary for a correct judgment of great practical affairs. If we would possess permanently a skilful and efficient body of functionaries - above all, a body able to originate and willing to adopt improvements; if we would not have our bureaucracy degenerate into a pedantocracy, this body must not engross all the occupations which form and cultivate the faculties required for the government of mankind.
base: When all the key talent is inside the leadership, it can slow down their thinking and stop them from moving forward. As a group, the officials work in a system full of old rules, which makes them lazy and stuck in habits. When they break away from that, their new ideas are often just copied from the top people. The only way to stop this from happening is to have people outside the group who are just as good looking at their work. This shows that there needs to be other ways to develop talent and give people real experience. To keep the officials smart and creative, not everything that helps them learn should be done by the group alone. This helps stop the system from just following old ways.
finetuned: The concentration of all the great talents of the country within the body of the governing class is a fatal obstacle to its mental activity and to its capacity for progress. As a body, the officials work in a system of rules which are too numerous and too unalterable to allow them to think; they are habitually doing the same thing, and when they do it differently it is usually the thing which has been thought by some distinguished man. The only check that can be put upon these two opposing tendencies - the tendency to become complacent and the tendency to be led by the nose by the leading men of the day - is the critical examination of the same men by equally able men outside the governing body. Hence the necessity for independent ways of cultivating talents and for giving them the experience of practical affairs which is needed for sound judgment. To ensure that the governing class shall be a perfect and inventive body of officials, it is necessary that not all the duties which are necessary to perfect the arts of government shall be the monopoly of the governing body itself.

title: On Liberty
input: A significant category of questions regarding the boundaries of government intervention will be addressed last. These questions are closely tied to the subject matter of this essay, although they do not strictly fall within its scope. The rationale behind non-interference in these instances does not revolve around the principle of liberty. Instead, the issue at hand is whether the government should provide assistance to individuals. The question revolves around the government's potential role in performing or facilitating certain actions for the benefit of individuals, as opposed to leaving such actions to be undertaken by those individuals themselves, either independently or through voluntary collaboration. Furthermore, this dilemma raises important considerations about the appropriate level of government involvement in the lives of citizens. Additionally, it highlights the need to balance individual autonomy with the potential benefits of government intervention.
human: I have reserved for the last place a large class of questions respecting the limits of government interference, which, though closely connected with the subject of this Essay, do not, in strictness, belong to it. These are cases in which the reasons against interference do not turn upon the principle of liberty: the question is not about restraining the actions of individuals, but about helping them: it is asked whether the government should do, or cause to be done, something for their benefit, instead of leaving it to be done by themselves, individually, or in voluntary combination.
base: A major group of questions about how much government can interfere will come later. These questions are closely related to the topic of this essay, even though they aren’t entirely part of it. The reason for not getting involved in these cases isn’t about freedom. The real issue is whether the government should help people. The question is whether the government should do certain things or help people do them, instead of letting people handle things on their own or through their own efforts. This problem also brings up important points about how much the government should be involved in people’s lives. It also shows the need to balance personal choice with the possible advantages of government action.
finetuned: A large class of questions, which will be considered in the last place, will now be touched on, but only as they are connected with the subject of this essay, though they are not included in its limits. The reason of non-interference in these cases is not liberty, but the question whether the Government should do anything for the people. It is, in short, the question whether the Government should do, or assist to do, anything for the benefit of the people, instead of leaving them to do it themselves, or to be done for them by their voluntary co-operation. The question is one of the proper sphere of Government, and one which has a bearing on the amount of its interference in the lives of the people.

title: On Liberty
input:
There exists a realm of action where society, as a collective, tends to have only an indirect interest, which includes aspects of a person's life and behavior that primarily impact themselves. While it is possible that these aspects may also affect others, this occurs only with their free and informed consent and participation. When referring to affecting oneself, it is important to note that this is in a direct and initial sense; what influences an individual may subsequently influence others through that individual. This potential for broader impact will be addressed later. Thus, this area represents the appropriate domain of personal liberty. 

It encompasses, first, the inner realm of consciousness, which calls for freedom of conscience in a broad sense. This includes the freedom to think and feel, as well as complete freedom of opinion and sentiment on all matters, whether practical, speculative, scientific, moral, or theological. The freedom to express and share opinions might appear to be governed by a different principle, since it pertains to an individual’s actions that involve others. However, it is often almost as significant as the freedom of thought itself and is largely based on similar reasoning, making it practically inseparable from it. Second, this principle advocates for the liberty of personal tastes and pursuits, allowing individuals to design their lives according to their own characters and to act as they wish, provided that their actions do not harm others, regardless of whether those others may perceive their choices as unwise or misguided. Third, from this individual liberty arises the freedom to form associations among individuals, enabling them to unite for any purpose that does not cause harm to others, assuming that those involved are of legal age and are not coerced or misled. In summary, the domain of human liberty encompasses individual thought, expression, personal pursuits, and the freedom to associate, all under the condition that these do not harm others.
human: But there is a sphere of action in which society, as distinguished from the individual, has, if any, only an indirect interest; comprehending all that portion of a person's life and conduct which affects only himself, or if it also affects others, only with their free, voluntary, and undeceived consent and participation. When I say only himself, I mean directly, and in the first instance: for whatever affects himself, may affect others through himself; and the objection which may be grounded on this contingency, will receive consideration in the sequel. This, then, is the appropriate region of human liberty. It comprises, first, the inward domain of consciousness; demanding liberty of conscience, in the most comprehensive sense; liberty of thought and feeling; absolute freedom of opinion and sentiment on all subjects, practical or speculative, scientific, moral, or theological. The liberty of expressing and publishing opinions may seem to fall under a different principle, since it belongs to that part of the conduct of an individual which concerns other people; but, being almost of as much importance as the liberty of thought itself, and resting in great part on the same reasons, is practically inseparable from it. Secondly, the principle requires liberty of tastes and pursuits; of framing the plan of our life to suit our own character; of doing as we like, subject to such consequences as may follow: without impediment from our fellow-creatures, so long as what we do does not harm them, even though they should think our conduct foolish, perverse, or wrong. Thirdly, from this liberty of each individual, follows the liberty, within the same limits, of combination among individuals; freedom to unite, for any purpose not involving harm to others: the persons combining being supposed to be of full age, and not forced or deceived.
base:
There is a space where society as a whole isn’t directly involved, and it includes parts of a person’s life that mainly affect themselves. These parts might also affect others, but only if those others agree and are aware. When it comes to things that affect a person directly, it’s the start of a chain. What influences one person can later influence others through that person. That bigger effect will come up later. So this is where personal freedom belongs.

It starts with the inner world of a person’s mind, which needs freedom of thought and feeling. That includes the right to think and feel anything, to have any opinion or emotion on any subject—practical, scientific, moral, or religious. The right to speak and share opinions might seem different because it involves others. But it’s just as important as the right to think, and it’s based on the same reasoning. So it’s almost like it’s tied together with the right to think.

Next, there’s the freedom to choose what you like and do what you want. People can live their lives according to their own nature, as long as their actions don’t hurt others. Even if others don’t see their choices as good, that’s okay. Third, from that freedom comes the right to form groups. People can come together for any purpose that doesn’t hurt others, as long as they’re old enough and not forced or tricked. In short, human freedom includes thinking, speaking, choosing, and joining groups, as long as they don’t hurt others.

There is a field of action where society, as a society, has only an indirect interest, which is in the life and conduct of an individual, which is primarily his own, and which, though it may affect others, does so only by their free and willing consent and co-operation. When we speak of affecting oneself, we have in view the direct and immediate sense; what affects an individual may affect others by the medium of that individual. The wider sphere of its influence will be considered hereafter. Thus this is the field of individual liberty.

It includes, first, the inner sphere of consciousness, in which we have the right of freedom of conscience in a wide sense, the right to think and to feel, the right to hold and to communicate complete freedom of opinion and sentiment on all matters, whether practical or speculative, scientific or moral, theological or not. The right to express and communicate opinions seems to be governed by a different principle, because it is the right of an individual to do something which affects others. But it is often almost as important as the right of thought itself, and is practically inseparable from it, being largely based on the same reasoning. Second, this principle advocates the liberty of personal tastes and pursuits, to design our lives as we think our characters warrant, to do as we please, so long as we injure no one, whether the injury be of consequence to the individual himself, or whether the injury be of consequence to others, who may think our choice unwise or mistaken. Third, from this individual liberty we have the freedom of association among individuals, to associate together for any purpose which does not injure others, assuming that those who associate are of legal age, and are not coerced or misled.

title: On Liberty
input: It is worth noting that there exist numerous acts which, while they may only cause direct harm to the individuals who engage in them, should not be subject to legal prohibition. However, when such acts are performed in public, they constitute a breach of social decorum and, consequently, may be legitimately restricted under the category of offenses against others. Offenses against decency exemplify this concept; further elaboration on these matters is unnecessary, particularly since they are only tangentially related to our primary topic. The objection to public display is equally applicable to many actions that are not inherently reprehensible or perceived as such.
human: Again, there are many acts which, being directly injurious only to the agents themselves, ought not to be legally interdicted, but which, if done publicly, are a violation of good manners and coming thus within the category of offences against others may rightfully be prohibited. Of this kind are offences against decency; on which it is unnecessary to dwell, the rather as they are only connected indirectly with our subject, the objection to publicity being equally strong in the case of many actions not in themselves condemnable, nor supposed to be so.
base: Many actions cause harm only to those who do them and shouldn’t be illegal. But when done in public, they break social rules and can be properly restricted as offenses against others. Examples like offenses against decency show this. There’s no need to go into more detail, since they’re only loosely connected to our main point. The same argument applies to many actions that aren’t really bad or seen that way.
finetuned: There are, indeed, many acts, which though they may injure only the persons who perform them, ought not to be made the subject of legal prohibition; but when performed in public, they are breaches of social manners, and may, therefore, be lawfully restrained, as offenses against others. Offences against decency are the most obvious instance of this; but no farther explanation of them is necessary, particularly as they only touch our subject at a distance. The objection to publicity, applies equally to many acts, which are not in themselves, or are not considered as, vicious.

title: The Time Machine
input:
You must follow my reasoning with considerable care. It is worth noting that I shall have to challenge one or two ideas that are almost universally accepted. For instance, the geometry that they taught you at school is founded upon a misconception.

Furthermore, is it not rather a substantial matter to expect us to begin upon? said Filby, an argumentative person with red hair.

Moreover, I do not mean to ask you to accept anything without reasonable ground for it. Additionally, you will soon concede as much as I require from you. It is worth noting that you know of course that a mathematical line, a line of no thickness, has no real existence. They taught you that? In essence, neither has a mathematical plane. These things are mere abstractions.

title: The Time Machine
input: Doubts began to arise, causing trouble. The question of why the Morlocks had taken the Time Machine came to mind, as it seemed likely they were responsible. This highlights the uncertainty surrounding the situation. Additionally, if the Eloi were indeed in a position of power, it was unclear why they could not return the machine. Furthermore, their intense fear of the dark was puzzling. In an attempt to gather more information, questions were posed to Weena about the Underworld. However, this line of inquiry was unsuccessful, as she initially failed to comprehend the questions and later refused to respond. The topic appeared to be unbearable for her, causing her to shiver. When pressed for answers, she became overwhelmed and cried. This suggests that the subject was deeply distressing for her. These tears were a rare sight in this era, and the only ones seen, apart from those of the narrator. Upon witnessing her distress, concern for the Morlocks subsided, and the focus shifted to comforting Weena. Ultimately, her tears were soon replaced with smiles and laughter, as a simple act, such as burning a match, was able to lift her spirits.
human: “Then came troublesome doubts. Why had the Morlocks taken my Time Machine? For I felt sure it was they who had taken it. Why, too, if the Eloi were masters, could they not restore the machine to me? And why were they so terribly afraid of the dark? I proceeded, as I have said, to question Weena about this Underworld, but here again I was disappointed. At first she would not understand my questions, and presently she refused to answer them. She shivered as though the topic was unendurable. And when I pressed her, perhaps a little harshly, she burst into tears. They were the only tears, except my own, I ever saw in that Golden Age. When I saw them I ceased abruptly to trouble about the Morlocks, and was only concerned in banishing these signs of her human inheritance from Weena’s eyes. And very soon she was smiling and clapping her hands, while I solemnly burnt a match.

Also, if the Eloi were in charge, it didn’t make sense why they couldn’t give the machine back. Their fear of the dark was weird too. To find out more, the narrator asked Weena about the Underworld. But she didn’t get it at first and then refused to answer. The topic was too hard for her, and she shivered. When asked again, she broke down and cried. That was rare back then, and the only other person crying was the narrator. Seeing her cry made the worry about the Morlocks go away. Instead, the focus was on comforting her. Soon after, her tears turned into smiles and laughter. Just burning a match was enough to make her happy again.
